title: S&P Sounds Alarm on Tether’s USDT as Risky Assets Surge to 28%
description: Tether has increased its gold holdings and entered public equities, but S&P says its growing exposure to risky assets remains concerning.
fullContent:
S&P Global Ratings has maintained its stability assessment of Tether’s USDT at 5 – weak. This is its lowest rating, citing a growing share of higher-risk assets in the reserves backing the dollar-pegged stablecoin.

By September 30th, these assets accounted for 28% of USDT in circulation.

Their share stood at 24% a year earlier, according to S&P. Tether held $191.5 billion in reserves against $183.5 billion in USDT circulation, which leaves a 104.3% backing ratio. However, S&P remains concerned about the assets held in those reserves.

Reserves Under Greater Scrutiny

Short-term US Treasury bills and Treasury-backed overnight reverse repurchase agreements accounted for 72% of the collateralization ratio, down from 75% in the previous review.

Meanwhile, Tether increased its gold holdings to about $19 billion, or 10% of USDT in circulation, from $12.9 billion a year earlier. It also added $4.2 billion in public equity investments, which represented 2% of circulation.

Bitcoin exposure, meanwhile, declined to $8.4 billion from $9.9 billion over the same period.

Other holdings include corporate bonds, secured loans, precious metals and investments whose composition and creditworthiness are not fully disclosed. S&P warned that significant declines in the value of these assets could leave USDT undercollateralized, particularly given the limited information available about some underlying investments.

The agency also highlighted gaps in transparency around reserve management, including the creditworthiness of custodians, counterparties, and banking providers.

Tether publishes quarterly reserve reports and obtains third-party attestations, but S&P noted that this is less frequent than the monthly reporting generally provided by other stablecoin issuers. Although the issuer completed its first full independent financial statement audit in 2026, the audited statements and accompanying report have not been made publicly available.

Regulatory Gaps and Limited Transparency

Another factor weighing on the assessment is regulatory and governance concerns.

Tether operates under El Salvador’s digital asset regulatory framework, which S&P considers less robust than those in the US and Europe, particularly because it does not require reserve assets to be segregated from the issuer’s other assets.

Limited disclosure about the separation of Tether’s wider business activities from USDT reserve management was another aspect that was brought into focus.

Direct redemption is restricted to verified customers, subject to a $100,000 minimum and additional fees. This leaves some holders dependent on secondary-market liquidity.

Despite these weaknesses, USDT has maintained a relatively stable dollar peg through periods of market stress and remains the largest stablecoin. Its circulation rose from about $158 billion in September 2025 to $184 billion a year later.

S&P said its assessment could improve if Tether reduces higher-risk holdings and provides more detailed information about its reserves and the institutions responsible for holding and managing them.

title: Dan Ives Calls Tech Selloff a Panic Moment but Anthropic IPO Shows Proof of Demand
description:
Dan Ives says the tech selloff is panic, not a broken AI thesis, as the Anthropic IPO closes up 17% on day one.
The post Dan Ives Calls Tech Selloff a Panic Moment but Anthropic IPO Shows Proof of Demand appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co says the six-day S&P 500 slide reflects panic, not a broken AI thesis. He points to the record Anthropic IPO, which raised $81 billion, as proof of demand.

Anthropic (ANT) closed its Nasdaq debut up 17% from its $83 offer price, well below a $115 intraday peak. However, the S&P 500 fell 2%, to 8.2% below last month’s record, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%.

Is This Selloff a Buying Opportunity or a Warning?

Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, spoke on CNBC‘s Power Lunch on Thursday. He partly blamed Nvidia (NVDA), China concerns and a short report on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) for the slide.

The AI buildout is under 15% complete, Ives said. The US, in his view, leads China in chips by two to three years.

Meanwhile, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), which tracks expected S&P 500 swings, stood at 28 during the segment. CNBC’s hosts said that was its highest level since March.

Still, he expects markets to look back on this stretch as an opportunity, like April 2025 and March 2020. Ives rejected a 2007-style bubble comparison, citing valuations and growth.

Ives made a similar case about the offering’s pricing.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia.”

Dan Ives, via PBS

Does the Anthropic IPO Demand Case Survive Its Costs?

The stock opened at $111.50, 34% above the offer, before closing at $97.17, CNBC reported.

However, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101 points as all three major indexes fell 2% or more, Yahoo reported.

In contrast, Anthropic still loses money under standard accounting rules and carries $6.2 billion in debt.

Moreover, signed contracts commit $900 billion to computing and infrastructure, with $70 billion due within a year, AP said.

OpenAI is not planning to list until next year, and Ives says Anthropic’s debut lays the groundwork. Holding above the $83 offer price may show whether public markets will keep financing AI spending on this scale.

title: WNBA star Caitlin Clark reveals unwavering loyalty to Notre Dame football after going incognito
description: Caitlin Clark told the "New Heights" podcast that Notre Dame recruited her, and she secretly attended their game against Miami earlier this month.
fullContent:
We all know that Caitlin Clark plays for the Indiana Fever, a WNBA team based in the same state as Notre Dame in South Bend.

After playing her college basketball at Iowa, Clark now plays much closer to her favorite college football team, the Notre Dame Fighting Irish. During an appearance this week on Jason Kelce and Travis Kelce's "New Heights" podcast, Clark spoke out about her Notre Dame loyalty, which dates back to her childhood.

Clark is such a staunch Fighting Irish supporter, that she admitted she wore a disguise to go see Notre Dame play Miami earlier this month. Notre Dame defeated Miami, then the No. 1 team in the nation, 31-24 in a game that was marked by late-game controversy.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I had on like a hat and sunglasses, and I was actually in the second to last row of like the normal bowl, like normal seats. Yeah, nobody knew, I mean some people knew," Clark said.

"People around me knew, but like the thing that's like the fun part about football in the fall is like just actually like being in the environment and like the experience of college football is so fun ... Tailgated a little bit. Jason Sudeikis was the guest picker that week. He was hanging out with us. He's a big, big Chiefs fan himself, so he's a great guy."

CAITLIN CLARK TELLS KYLIE KELCE SHE WANTS 'TO BE LOYAL TO THE RED' AFTER COLTS' BLUE JERSEY CONTROVERSY

The Fighting Irish women's basketball team also recruited Clark as she was preparing to take the leap from high school to the college level.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I try to make it to, like, one Notre Dame game a year. I grew up a Notre Dame fan. I wanted to go to Notre Dame," she noted. "They recruited me. It was between Notre Dame and Iowa, and then I picked Iowa. But Notre Dame is just so cool – the history of everything. And then a night game, you're playing the number one team in the country."

Clark also made a surprise appearance at Penn’s men’s basketball game against Illinois in Champaign on Nov. 5. Fran McCaffery, the father of Clark’s boyfriend, Connor McCaffery, is in his second season as Penn's head coach.

Many of the Illinois players did not realize Clark was in attendance until after the game, prompting a jaw-dropping reaction from Quentin Coleman. "Wait, Caitlin was in the building?" Coleman said. "Yoooo! I gotta tell my sister, bro."

NOTRE DAME FOOTBALL HOLDS MICHIGAN STATE TO 167 TOTAL YARDS IN 27-10 HOME VICTORY

Clark also showed off her football fandom earlier this year as a celebrity guest picker on ESPN’s "College GameDay." She also helped energize the Iowa fans that were on hand before the Hawkeyes' matchup with Ohio State.

Clark earned her third consecutive WNBA All-Star selection this year. Clark and the Fever were eliminated in the first round of the playoffs after losing to the Las Vegas Aces.

title: Bitcoin Could Suffer a 1929-Style Crash Ahead of the Anthropic IPO, BitMEX Co-Founder Says
description: BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes warns Bitcoin could see a 1929-style crash before the Anthropic IPO. Support near $59,000 is the level that tests his call.
fullContent:
Three Things to Know

  • Arthur Hayes, the BitMEX co-founder, warned Bitcoin could suffer a 1929-style crash before the Anthropic IPO.
  • Hayes named no price target, so the nearest chart support serves as the practical test.
  • A daily close back above the converging moving averages would undercut his bearish call.

Arthur Hayes has a grim warning for Bitcoin holders. The BitMEX co-founder said the largest cryptocurrency could face a crash on the scale of 1929 before AI firm Anthropic goes public, though he expects authorities to step in.

The call lands while Bitcoin is already deep in a monthlong slide and sellers control the trend. Traders now face one question. Will the selling turn into panic, or has most of the damage already been done?

Hayes Sees a 1929 Moment Before Anthropic Lists

Hayes, who co-founded crypto derivatives exchange BitMEX, used the phrase "1929-style" to describe the risk ahead of the Anthropic initial public offering.

Hayes did not attach a price target or a firm date to the call. His only time frame is the run-up to the listing of the artificial intelligence company. The comparison to 1929 points to a sudden, broad collapse that drags on every risky asset.

He added a caveat. Hayes said authorities won't let such a crash happen. In his view, officials would step in before the damage spreads too far, which would put a ceiling on any slide.

That leaves readers with two claims to weigh. One is a severe drop, and the other is a rescue that limits it.

$59K Is the Last Floor Before Hayes' Crash Thesis

Bitcoin (BTC) daily price with the nearest support (green) and resistance (red). Source: TradingView

Bitcoin traded near $62,000, flat on the day. It sits below its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, which both stand near $75,000. These averages track the typical price over recent months, and right now they act as a ceiling. Trend strength readings point to a real trend, and sellers are leading it.

Momentum sides with Hayes for now. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, sits near 20, which is deeply oversold. MACD also remains below its signal line, so momentum is still pointing down. Readings this stretched often come before a relief bounce, though they cannot say when one starts.

On the daily chart, the nearest support sits near $59,000, about 5% below the current price. The data shows no mapped level beneath it. A break there would leave the market without a clear floor. Resistance sits at those averages, roughly 21% higher, with $80,000 behind it.

Hayes gave no target, so a close below $59,000 is the practical test of his crash call. A move back above $75,000 would undercut it.

What Other Signals Say About the Slide

The recent pace of losses tells its own story. Bitcoin has shed about 13% in a week and roughly a quarter of its value in a month.

Those numbers mean the selling Hayes describes is already well underway. Buyers have stepped back for weeks, and each rally attempt has faded.

That cuts both ways for his call. The market keeps trending lower, which matches his warning. Yet a drop this deep also means much of the fear may already be in the price. A true 1929-style collapse would need fresh panic on top of losses traders have already absorbed.

Watch Whether the Floor Cracks or the Averages Return

Two signals will settle the question. Hayes gains ground if Bitcoin posts a daily close under that nearest support while momentum keeps falling. That would leave no mapped floor below.

His call loses force if price climbs back above the converging moving averages. Reclaiming that zone would show buyers back in control.

title: Senate Republicans break through Washington gridlock with massive American energy, data center overhaul
description: Senate Republicans advanced a sweeping permitting bill to speed environmental review, expand the electric grid and limit legal challenges on projects.
fullContent:
Senate Republicans scored a major win after advancing a massive bill that would overhaul America’s permitting system in a bid to turbocharge infrastructure and energy development in the country.

The Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on a major bipartisan vote Thursday night. The legislation went through fits and starts over the last few months, until a bipartisan coalition, with buy-in from the White House, formed to tinker with the final product.

At the 30,000-foot level, the sweeping package would accelerate environmental review of projects, limit legal challenges, protect approved projects, expand the electric grid and streamline energy development in all fields — like oil, gas and renewables.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said when the bill was introduced in September.

The bill also tackles an issue that was front and center for voters across the country: data centers.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the Democratic lead on the legislation, pushed for stronger language in the bill that would shield ratepayers from higher costs that stem from data center development and their usage of electricity.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

That comes after Republicans tried to ram through similar safeguards before the election with a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Democrats argued lacked real enforcement teeth.

"This process will mean that we develop responsibly. It will mean more jobs. It will mean cheaper energy," Heinrich said. "It will mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that's a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not a suggestion, an actual law."

The provision covers data centers with a demand of at least 20 megawatts of power, and would require them to cover the cost of additional power for them to run, financial guarantees covering costs to build or upgrade facilities, to pay the tab if they leave an area for unpaid infrastructure costs, allow states to charge higher rates to reduce other customers’ bills and tack on power supply conditions.

DEMS KILL REPUBLICAN'S CHANCES OF LOWERING AMERICANS' ELECTRICITY BILLS IN KEY ELECTION FLASHPOINT

Meanwhile, whether the legislation makes it through the House is an open question.

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who was appointed to the position earlier this year to replace Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and has made permitting reform his primary policy issue, told Fox News Digital that there were "a lot of good supporters on both sides of the aisle in the House." But he worried about attendance issues in the lower chamber.

"A lot of the language that's in here came right out of a lot of the House’s work," Armstrong said. "So, I think there'll be some support. I just hope we have people, you know, show up in the numbers that we need to vote for it."

title: Tom Lee Says Anthropic Debut Selloff Feels Like ‘Max Pain’: Will Tech Rebound?
description:
Tom Lee says the Anthropic debut selloff feels like max pain, as ANT slides from its open and the S&P 500 drops 2%.
The post Tom Lee Says Anthropic Debut Selloff Feels Like ‘Max Pain’: Will Tech Rebound? appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Anthropic (ANT) opened at $111.50 in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, then slid to $97.17 as the S&P 500 fell 2.02% for a sixth straight session. Fundstrat’s Tom Lee says the selloff feels like max pain for tech but should reward patient investors.

AI shares rallied early on the debut, but the bid faded and all seven Magnificent Seven stocks, the largest US tech names, closed lower. Neoclouds, newer data center operators that rent out AI computing power, also fell, with Nebius down 9.39% and CoreWeave down 6.11%.

Is Max Pain Already Here for Tech?

ANT closed $14.17 above its $83 initial public offering (IPO) price but $14.33 under its opening trade, after an intraday high of $115.10.

The $81.3 billion offering topped the $75 billion SpaceX raised at pricing in June, but SpaceX’s total later grew to $85.7 billion after underwriters bought extra shares, TechCrunch reported. Anthropic’s figure does not include any extra shares its underwriters may still sell.

Lee, managing partner and head of research at Fundstrat, told CNBC’s Closing Bell that the moment resembles Cisco in 1997. He said the stock fell almost 50% in three months, then reached about $18 a year later.

“we are at that moment where it feels like max pain”

Tom Lee, via CNBC

In October, Lee said the AI selloff was nearing its end, citing yields below 5%, and the Nasdaq slid into a correction within two weeks.

The host pressed Lee on neocloud borrowing costs and on Federal Reserve minutes, released Wednesday, that put AI financing risks in focus. Lee replied that corporations upgrading their infrastructure, not speculative investors, may end up funding demand for compute, and he raised JPMorgan as a potential neocloud.

Can Corporate Budgets Replace Speculative Money?

With the 10-year Treasury yield back above the 5% line Lee cited in October, at 5.05%, the AI buildout hinges on whether corporate budgets can replace speculative capital.

Lee has also blamed an earlier selloff on fears over Democratic gains in Congress, with newly elected lawmakers set to take office in 2027.

title: Army delays controlled detonation of unstable bomb-making chemical in Iowa
description: The Army postponed the controlled detonation of 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, citing a temperature drop.
fullContent:
The U. S. Army postponed Friday's planned controlled detonation of five tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at an Iowa munitions plant until Monday, Nov. 23, amid an incoming temperature drop, environmental lawsuits and a call to delay the blast from Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle directed Army Materiel Command to push back the operation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, placing the detonation at the latest possible window before the weather shifts.

"Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23," Telle said in a statement on X.

IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," the statement added.

The pause came after Reynolds urged the Army to delay the operation amid growing public safety concerns in the region, while environmental groups filed lawsuits seeking to halt the planned detonation.

The decision delays a temporary evacuation for the roughly 400 residents of Middletown, who had been advised to leave their homes Friday morning due to "the potential for localized window damage" and a dust plume containing lead particles.

Crews are preparing to detonate 68 drums of degraded lead azide, a chemical used to set off munitions that had been stored in bunkers at the plant for more than 20 years. Army officials discovered in March that water had evaporated from the barrels' stabilizing bath, allowing the material to recrystallize and become too unstable to handle or relocate safely.

"The recrystallization of lead azide has created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," the Environmental Protection Agency said earlier this month when approving an emergency permit for the blast.

CALIFORNIA OFFICIALS WARN MASSIVE CHEMICAL TANK WILL LIKELY SPILL THOUSANDS OF GALLONS OR 'BLOW UP'

An Army smoke model released Tuesday projected the plume could reach 25 miles north to Wapello, Iowa, and spread across parts of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland and playgrounds. The model also noted that "Children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure."

The Army said it will continue coordinating with the EPA and state and local officials to share updated safety and evacuation guidance ahead of Monday's rescheduled detonation.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

title: Jeff Bezos Laughs Off Merging Amazon and His $41 Billion AI Startup as Elon Musk Explores Tesla-SpaceX Deal: 'Such a Funny Idea’
description:
Some billionaires are weighing megamergers. Others are laughing at the question.
Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos was asked this week if his ventures could someday be tied together the way Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk is trying to combine his businesses. Those ventures include AI startup Prometheus, rocket company Blue Origin and possibly Amazon itself.
He didn’t sound like a man drafting merger paperwork.
Separate Companies, Separate Punchlines
“That’s such a such a funny idea,” Bezos said Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event. “I don’t see that right now.”
Then he added the line every corporate lawyer loves to hear. “I have nothing to announce,” he said.
The question wasn’t random. During Space Exploration Technologies Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:SPCX) third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 20, CEO Musk said that SpaceX and Tesla had each formed special committees of independent directors to study a possible combination.
Musk also said a deal isn’t guaranteed and would need approval from Tesla shareholders.
Bezos Would Rather Build Toaster Ovens
Bezos spent much of the same appearance talking up Prometheus, the AI startup he runs as co-CEO with Vik Bajaj. The company raised $12 billion at a $41 billion valuation in June, Bezos said at the time.
His pitch is that chatbots trained on the internet can’t do everything.
“So, I could read a thousand books on how to be a great gymnast and I would still be a terrible gymnast or a thousand books on how to be a dancer and I still couldn’t dance,” Bezos said.
He then posed a thought experiment about history’s greatest physicists, including Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein. “Take those six brilliant physicists, put them in a room together and say, ‘Build me a toaster oven.’ They would have no idea how to do it,” he said.
That’s why Prometheus is training specialized models for engineering. Bezos said the company’s tools are designing analog chips and radios in 12 hours. He estimated the same work would take a team of 10 to 20 people six to nine months.
“We have 250 people now,” Bezos said.
He also described a Prometheus teammate who previously worked on the Mars helicopter at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. That teammate asked the tools to redesign the aircraft with a single prompt. Bezos said the system tried quadcopters, counterrotating helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft before landing on something that looked very much like the real Mars helicopter.
“The entire manufacturing economy is going to be transformed by AI in the coming years,” Bezos said.
One Empire, Many Org Charts
Musk wants his rockets and cars under one roof. Bezos, at least for now, seems happier letting each company chase its own moonshot while he goes all in on AI.

title: Feds release brazen heist video, charge 14 in alleged $22.5M California freight train theft ring
description: Fourteen suspects face federal charges in an alleged $22.5 million cargo theft scheme targeting 36 freight trains in Southern California.
fullContent:
At least 14 suspects have been federally charged with orchestrating a $22.5 million cargo theft scheme that targeted at least 36 freight trains in Southern California, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California announced Thursday.

The crew's leader was identified as Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, who allegedly ran the operation alongside his father and two uncles.

Officials also released video of the brazen heist that appeared to have been filmed by some of the crew members. In the clip, members are seen sawing through cargo doors, grabbing boxes and flashing peace signs as they ransacked the trains.

"The scale of the theft is staggering," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said. "We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash."

CARGO THEFT HITS EVERYTHING FROM LEGO TO TEQUILA. WE NEED THE SENATE TO HELP STOP IT

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS IN STOLEN GOODS RECOVERED AT A USED CAR LOT AFTER ADULT TOY COMPANY PURCHASE

From February 2024 to August 2026, Nathan Angel allegedly led a group of co-conspirators in targeting freight trains carrying high-value goods for resale on the black market.

The trains reportedly carried Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, electronics and other products that entered the U.S. through the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from international destinations.

According to prosecutors, Nathan Angel and his co-conspirators allegedly planned their thefts in advance by selecting specific locations along railroad tracks where they could force trains to stop.

Once the trains reached these preselected locations, members of the group cut the air hoses to trigger an emergency stop, officials alleged.

As the trains came to a halt, other crew members allegedly used trucks or vans to drive to the designated locations and board the trains, while additional members acted as lookouts.

The alleged thieves then transported the goods to stash houses, including properties belonging to some of the suspects.

The crew then coordinated their thefts through Instagram while discussing resale prices for the stolen products, prosecutors alleged.

NEARLY $1M IN GRADED TRADING CARDS STOLEN FROM FEDEX TRUCK OUTSIDE PSA FACILITY IN SANTA ANA

Officials said one buyer was a representative of a Los Angeles-based business known as a sneaker and streetwear resale brand. The business was not an authorized Nike reseller, officials said.

That business alone reportedly generated more than $1 million for the crew by purchasing thousands of pairs of stolen Nike sneakers between May 2025 and October 2025.

The crew leader's family members named in the case include his father, Daniel Angel, 38, of East Los Angeles, and his uncles, Rodolfo Angel, 23, and Jose Luis Angel, 23, both of East Los Angeles.

The other defendants include Donta Hedgeman, 27, Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, Daniel Garcia, 36, Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, Angel Sanchez, 24, Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, Fredy Marquina, 25, Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, and Ricardo Mares, 32.

"Train robberies cause enormous economic damage because of the valuable cargo involved. These defendants face long federal prison sentences if convicted. All are presumed innocent until proven guilty," Essayli said.

The arrests followed a 14-month investigation that involved the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program and the IRS Criminal Investigation.

If convicted, the defendants face maximum federal prison sentences of five years for conspiracy and 10 years per theft count. Additionally, each count of violence against railroad cars carries a maximum penalty of life in prison.

title: Deion Sanders receives 'about five' death threats every day as Colorado football coach
description: Deion Sanders gets about five death threats a day, per The Athletic, which obtained 15 closed harassment cases since he took over Colorado football.
fullContent:
Just a few years ago, Colorado’s football program had largely been forgotten. Then Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders arrived in Boulder, bringing his larger-than-life personality and celebrity to the program.

Colorado’s on-field results under Sanders have been uneven, but his tenure has also been marked by significant off-field challenges. Sanders has continued coaching while managing serious health issues. More recently, police records obtained by The Athletic detailed how his personal safety has been at risk at times.

According to a September report, Sanders regularly received death threats. At one point, he said he was receiving "about five" threats per day. Public records from Boulder shed light on how authorities handled many of those situations.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In May 2023, a pair of university police officers waited for Sanders outside his office. Once the two-time Super Bowl winner met the officers, they told Sanders about a series of threatening voicemails on a Colorado football ticket office phone line that mentioned him.

At the time, Sanders was just six months into the job and had yet to coach a game. "I guess this confirms what you are working on," Sanders told Evis McGee, a member of his personal security team, after learning about the voicemails, per the police report.

DEION SANDERS SAYS ALLEGED $50,000 OFFER TO SILENCE CRITICS WAS 'A JOKE' AMID COLORADO'S STRUGGLES

The voicemails proved not to be an isolated incident. The Athletic ultimately discovered 15 closed University of Colorado police cases involving harassment or suspicious activity directed at Sanders since he left Jackson State and was named the Buffaloes head coach. Two additional cases remain open, with records unavailable, and most stem from 2023.

In a YouTube video posted in January by Sanders’ son, Deion Jr., Michael Rhodes warned players to "be mindful of who comes in [the facility] with you, especially on the elevator." Rhodes delivered those comments during an introductory meeting ahead of the 2026 season.

"Don’t let somebody coerce you into scanning them up on the floor, because everybody’s trying to get to Coach Prime," he continued. Rhodes is the head of Sanders' university-paid security team.

"Some people say, ‘Coach, what do you need a head of security for?’ We get death threats all the time," said Sanders. "Why? I’m a Black man making it happen. … That stuff is real.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"How many death threats we get?" Sanders was shown in the video asking Rhodes.

He responded: "About five every day."

MATT RHULE DRAWS THE LINE AFTER FAN VERBALLY ATTACKS HIS 13-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER FOLLOWING LATEST NEBRASKA LOSS

Colorado athletics said its security efforts involve Sanders’ personal security team as well as the CU Boulder Division of Public Safety.

"The safety of Coach Prime is our top priority, and we take every threat seriously," the athletics department said in a statement. "CU Athletics works closely with the CU Boulder Division of Public Safety to coordinate security efforts with Coach Prime’s entire team, including his security detail, and respond appropriately to reported threats."

Nearly half of the 15 closed cases The Athletic reviewed were found to have ties to one individual who repeatedly mailed threatening letters. The letters contained incoherent passages and biblical references, along with racist remarks directed at Sanders.

Colorado has two games remaining on its 2026 schedule and needs to win both to become bowl eligible, something that seemed completely out of reach earlier in the season. Sanders led the Buffaloes to a 42-32 upset of Houston last week.

title: Bitcoin Falls to Mining Cost Level as Hashrate Nears Record and Indicators Flip Bearish
description:
Bitcoin hits its $62,000 mining cost as hashrate nears a record. See why on-chain data still points to more downside.
The post Bitcoin Falls to Mining Cost Level as Hashrate Nears Record and Indicators Flip Bearish appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC) trades at $61,568, now below the $62,862 an average major miner pays to produce one coin. Network computing power remains near its peak, yet on-chain data now leans negative.

The price is down 2.6% over the past 24 hours. It sits about 50% below its October 2025 all-time high of $126,080.

Bitcoin Mining Cost Floor Faces Its Third Test of 2026

CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju flagged the move on November 18. He warned that a break lower could pressure public miners and their institutional backers.

The estimate comes from CryptoQuant data based on MARA Holdings filings. It puts the average cost of mining one BTC at $62,862 for the third quarter of 2026.

This marks the third time BTC has tested the line this year. In February, the price dropped to the cost level near $64,000. In June and July, it briefly slipped below the roughly $60,000 quarterly cost before recovering.

However, the figure reflects one company rather than the whole industry. MARA ranks among the largest miners, so smaller operators likely face higher costs and thinner margins. For comparison, JPMorgan’s production cost estimate stood at $85,000 in late September.

Hashrate Nears Its Record as Miners Keep Investing

Ki Young Ju also noted that hashrate remains high despite the squeeze. In his view, public miners are still betting on a long-term bull market.

Glassnode data supports that reading. The 30-day average hashrate stands near 1.02 zettahashes per second (ZH/s). That is less than 10% below the record of about 1.1 ZH/s set in November 2025.

More notably, hashrate and price have moved in opposite directions. Since early October, hashrate has climbed more than 10% from about 915 exahashes per second (EH/s). Over the same period, BTC has lost more than 25%.

Meanwhile, the network shows no sign of miner capitulation. In past downturns, falling hashrate signaled operators switching off unprofitable machines. That has not happened, even as some miners shift power to Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Still, hashrate tends to lag price. Mining hardware is ordered months in advance. Part of the recent growth may reflect machines bought when BTC traded near $87,000.

On-Chain Indicators Flip Bearish, Analyst Warns

In contrast, on-chain data paints a weaker near-term picture. Julio Moreno is Head of Research at CryptoQuant and a member of BeInCrypto’s Market Intelligence Experts Council. He says the market has turned.

There’s no sugarcoating it, by basically all metrics, Bitcoin returned to a bearish phase.

According to Moreno, both spot and speculative demand have contracted sharply since late October. He added that the analysts CryptoQuant tracks are the most bearish since November 2025.

Price has also broken almost every key on-chain and technical support, he noted. The warning adds to other bearish signals that appeared after BTC’s rebound earlier this week.

His chart of long-term holder (LTH) spending by price level shows where the remaining support sits. The densest 2026 cluster lies between $62,500 and $65,000. On many days at those prices, 30-day LTH spending reached 250,000 to 475,000 BTC.

Below $62,000, that activity thins out sharply. Moreno acknowledged some capitulation, with holders realizing large daily losses. However, he warned there is still room for more selling.

Bitcoin Mining Cost and $62,000 Floor

Three separate signals now converge near the same price. The mining cost stands at $62,862, the recent low at aorund $61,00, and the densest LTH cluster begins at $62,500.

A sustained break below $62,000 would remove both the miner floor and the strongest remaining on-chain support. In that case, $60,000 becomes the next level to watch, followed by the 2026 low near $57,700.

On the upside, BTC would need to reclaim $65,000 to clear the LTH cluster. The next heavy zone, between $76,000 and $82,000, could then act as resistance.

Macro conditions add pressure. US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have recorded about $2.6 billion in net outflows in November. Minutes from the Federal Reserve’s latest meeting have also revived talk of a December rate hike.

Both camps may prove right. Moreno still sees BTC in a value zone, yet he cautions that a recovery could take time.

Yes, Bitcoin price is in a value zone, but, historically, a bottoming process and subsequent recovery has taken months, even if there are short-term rallies in the process.

Miners, for now, appear willing to wait out that process. Whether the $62,000 floor holds may decide how long they have to.

title: NBA icon Russell Westbrook hands out 1,500 Thanksgiving meals in the rain for kids in LA
description: Russell Westbrook braved rain at Jesse Owens Park giving out 1,500 Thanksgiving meals and winter coats through the Why Not? Foundation in South LA.
fullContent:
Retired NBA icon Russell Westbrook spent Thursday afternoon in steady rain at Jesse Owens Park in South Los Angeles, handing out 1,500 Thanksgiving meals, groceries and winter coats to local families.

Three months after retiring from the NBA, the former league MVP worked the distribution line himself through his Why Not? Foundation.

Video shared (via NBA reporter Joey Linn) showed Westbrook loading food packages alongside volunteers in the rain. Westbrook grew up playing at Jesse Owens Park, and three years ago he partnered with the Los Angeles Clippers to refurbish and reopen its main basketball court in his honor.

Thursday marked the foundation's 14th annual Thanksgiving giveaway and its largest yet. Volunteers packed the supplies Tuesday at It's Bigger Than Us in Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza, backed by LA County Parks and Recreation, Los Angeles County, and Cal Dental USA.

The expanded budget came from Westbrook's sixth annual Why Not? Poker Night in Las Vegas in September, which raised over $900,500 and pushed the event's six-year total near $3 million.

"We started this at Jesse Owens Park 14 years ago, and we show up every November," Westbrook said.

"This is home. We've been blessed with more this year, so why not give more back to the community?"

FORMER CLIPPERS STAR WARNS OF TEAM'S UPHILL BATTLE AFTER BRUTAL KAWHI LEONARD SALARY CAP PUNISHMENT

Westbrook stepped away this summer after 18 seasons across seven franchises, finishing with the Sacramento Kings.

He retired as the NBA's all-time triple-doubles leader, the 2017 MVP, a nine-time All-Star, a two-time scoring champion, a three-time assists leader, and an Olympic gold medalist.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

FORMER NFL PASS RUSHER ALDON SMITH'S LAST ACT BEFORE HIS DEATH WAS DONATING FOOD FOR THE HOMELESS

Analysts spent years debating his play on the court, yet his commitment to South Los Angeles since founding his charity in 2012 has never wavered.

Even in retirement, Westbrook stood in the rain to make sure 1,500 families had Thanksgiving dinner and winter coats.

title: Michael Burry Says He Warned on AI With NVIDIA and CoreWeave: Big Short Déjà Vu?
description:
Michael Burry says he warned investors about Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius as shares fell, while holding bearish puts.
The post Michael Burry Says He Warned on AI With NVIDIA and CoreWeave: Big Short Déjà Vu? appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Michael Burry says he warned investors about Nvidia (NVDA), CoreWeave (CRWV), and Nebius (NBIS), whose shares all fell on Thursday and have been subject to a recent AI rout. He says he never told anyone to short them.

Burry’s post stops short of a sell call, yet his Substack positions lean bearish across the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductors. Nebius holders lost 9.4% Thursday, CoreWeave holders 6.1%, and Nvidia holders 3.3%.

Was Michael Burry’s Nvidia Warning a Sell Signal?

“Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all. I didn’t say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell.”

Michael Burry, a former Scion Asset Management fund manager, wrote on X Thursday.

However, TipRanks reported that he holds Nvidia puts struck at $140, expiring in February 2027.

In a Nov. 12 Substack post, he said he doubled his put options on the Nasdaq-100 index. A put pays off if the underlying price drops.

He rebuilt part of his put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which counts Nvidia among its top holdings.

Why Are Nvidia’s Partners Exposed?

CoreWeave and Nebius operate as neoclouds, selling artificial intelligence (AI) developers access to Nvidia-powered servers.

Burry argued that CoreWeave, Nebius, chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, and equipment maker ASML leaned on Nvidia’s market power.

Meanwhile, Nvidia shares have fallen 19% since Nov. 8, CNBC reported Thursday.

That was when co-founder Jensen Huang admitted extramarital affairs to staff. He resigned as CEO four days later.

However, revenue still jumped 103% to $115.8 billion in Nvidia’s first post-Huang earnings report.

In contrast, interim CEO Colette Kress has rejected neocloud concerns, saying the biggest cloud operators are not pulling back.

Does the Big Short Comparison Hold Up?

Burry made his name betting against the 2008 housing bubble and issued an earlier market warning in October.

His reported Nvidia puts carry a $140 strike, against a $145.98 Thursday close, Fool data show. The shares sit 39% below their October high, even as quarterly revenue more than doubled.

His Nasdaq-100 puts run into early 2027. Therefore, that window will test his view that Nvidia’s market power has entered a new phase.

title: LSU poked the SEC bear, then folded: RJ Luis benched after conference leaders discussed expulsion or boycott
description: Sources tell OutKick SEC schools weighed boycotting games against LSU and expelling the Tigers before the school benched RJ Luis amid the legal fight.
fullContent:
One day after Will Wade sent RJ Luis onto the court, LSU has backed down from its latest fight with the SEC.

LSU President Wade Rousse announced late Thursday afternoon that the Tigers would no longer play Luis, abruptly reversing course after the former professional basketball player scored 11 points in Wednesday night’s win over Louisiana-Monroe.

"In my role as president of the LSU System, after further review, I have instructed LSU men's basketball coach Will Wade not to play RJ Luis," Rousse said.

LANE KIFFIN’S ROSTER FIGHT SET THE STAGE, WILL WADE JUST THREW A GRENADE IN LSU-SEC WAR WITH RJ LUIS

That’s quite the turnaround from the message Wade delivered after Wednesday’s game.

"He was eligible, and he played," Wade said.

For a school locked in a federal lawsuit with the SEC over the roster battle involving Lane Kiffin’s football program in September, playing Luis was another escalation.

Less than 24 hours later, LSU put down its sword related to the basketball player.

Not even 24 hours after RJ Luis scored 11 points in the LSU win, the Tigers waived the white flag regarding this fight that involved their basketball team.

Why the sudden change of heart?

SEC presidents were already scheduled to hold a call Thursday afternoon to discuss several topics. But after Luis played Wednesday night, the conversation was set to take on a different tone.

ATTORNEY COMPARES SEC COMMISSIONER GREG SANKEY TO ‘KIM JONG’ IN LSU-RJ LUIS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUIT

Multiple sources told OutKick that options including SEC schools boycotting games against LSU and renewed discussions about potentially expelling the Tigers from the conference were back on the table.

"That was the final straw for SEC leaders, they were ready to penalize them (LSU) in some form or fashion," one source familiar with the discussions told OutKick. "You can only poke the bear so many times before they decide to pounce, and they (SEC Presidents and Chancellors) had seen enough nonsense from LSU.

"Who knows if they would have actually boycotted games, or even tried. But, lawyers from schools within the conference were going through their options. This whole thing is just annoying. Like, get your sh-t together, and I mean everyone involved."

SEC FILES BOMBSHELL LAWSUIT AGAINST LSU, LANE KIFFIN WHILE PRO PLAYERS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE ELIGIBILITY IN COURT

Sources also told OutKick that SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey spoke with Rousse on Thursday afternoon before the scheduled presidents’ meeting, delivering a blunt and honest assessment of the thinking of conference leaders of what could happen if LSU continued playing Luis.

The message apparently landed.

Less than two hours after the conversation with Sankey and consultations with its own general counsel, LSU announced that Luis would no longer play. Rousse did not participate in the full call with the other SEC presidents.

LSU’s decision does not necessarily mean Luis is finished fighting.

The former professional football players involved in the separate LSU eligibility case are still considering a civil lawsuit against the SEC over what they contend was interference with their court-ordered ability to play.

Could Luis pursue some type of damages of his own? A statement from one of his attorneys suggests this dispute could be far from over.

"The SEC's decision to threaten a member with expulsion if it plays an eligible student-athlete is reprehensible and seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him," one of RJ Luis's attorneys, Elliot Abrams, said in a statement.

COLLEGE ATHLETICS' LATEST MESS: COURT ORDERS SAY PRO ATHLETES CAN PLAY, BUT SEC AND BIG TEN READY TO FIGHT

The latest showdown began last Friday, when a Baton Rouge judge granted Luis a preliminary injunction. The scope of that order — and whether its protections extended to LSU playing him — became a central point of contention.

In a statement Monday, the SEC said it would abide by the order and would not punish LSU for rostering Luis.

Playing him was another matter.

On Tuesday, the conference made clear that it disagreed with LSU’s interpretation of the court order.

"LSU’s decision today to rely on its own interpretation of the Court’s order to justify its actions is inconsistent with the expectations and responsibilities of [SEC membership]. This is a deeply concerning and disappointing development."

The SEC wants to enforce its membership rules. LSU relied on its interpretation of a Baton Rouge judge’s order to put a former professional player on the court.

On Wednesday night, the Tigers tested how far they could push that argument.

By Thursday afternoon, they had their answer.

This basketball dispute is another chapter in a fight that had already spilled into federal court.

Three months ago, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit against LSU as Sankey testified in a Baton Rouge courtroom in the case brought by Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who were seeking to play football for Kiffin’s Tigers.

The federal case has since produced its own stream of legal jabs.

On Wednesday, the SEC asked a judge to strike language from LSU’s motion to dismiss in which the school’s attorneys accused the conference of making "hallucinated" claims against a defendant.

A judge ordered LSU’s lawyers to issue a public apology through a press release. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill pushed back in a filing, telling the court that would not happen.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

That same day, attorney Tony Clayton, representing Luis, filed a motion seeking to hold the SEC in contempt over the conference’s Tuesday statement.

So, yes, there were already plenty of reasons for tension between LSU and its conference before Wade sent Luis into Wednesday’s game.

Playing him amounted to throwing another grenade into an ongoing legal battle.

Now, LSU has retreated on the basketball front, leaving Luis sidelined while the broader fight continues.

Will that open the door for peace talks between LSU and the SEC?

Given the lawsuits, threats and courtroom clashes hanging over this relationship, I wouldn’t count on a ceasefire just yet.

title: Senate passes bipartisan bill to make data centers pay for their energy use
description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.
The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.
Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.
Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.
However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. 
“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.
Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
Democrats push for amendments
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.
Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.
“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.
Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”
The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.
Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.
“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government. 
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said. 
The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation. 
The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.
Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate
Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered. 
Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife. 
“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”
Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said. 
Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.” 
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure. 
But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.
___
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.
This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/senate-vote-bill-speed-permitting-020439514.html

title: Trump’s National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross fired amid widespread tech outages
description: President Donald Trump backed the firing of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross over cybersecurity credentials, with Kirsten A. Davies stepping in.
fullContent:
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out after President Donald Trump backed his firing over concerns he lacked the cybersecurity credentials for the job, Fox News has confirmed.

Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will step into the position in an acting capacity. 

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

An administration official separately told Fox News that Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. Cairncross took office Aug. 4, 2025, after Senate confirmation, and the exact date of his departure remains unclear.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

Senior administration officials welcomed Davies' appointment on X.

"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity," Rubio wrote.

Clayton praised her background, writing, "With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote, "The Department congratulates Kirsten Davies on her new role as the National Cyber Director. Throughout her tenure at DOW, she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape."

US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT

Davies thanked Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Hegseth in her own post on X, calling the moment a critical juncture for U.S. technology.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency. 

A Nov. 13 Federal Aviation Administration outage triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight cancellations after contractor work on air traffic control wiring overloaded the system.

Administration officials have pushed back against speculation that hackers or foreign adversaries were behind the disruptions. Rubio said Tuesday that officials found "zero evidence" tying the incidents together or to malicious actors, while Clayton said the outages appeared linked to routine software patches and system upgrades rather than a coordinated cyberattack.

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

The Office of the National Cyber Director and Cairncross did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Nikkei Slides 4% as Anthropic's Debut Triggers AI Sell-Off in Tokyo
description:
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 4.2% as SoftBank and chip stocks sank after Anthropic's Nasdaq debut.
The post Nikkei Slides 4% as Anthropic's Debut Triggers AI Sell-Off in Tokyo appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 4.23% at 56,931.75 in Friday trading as AI stocks sold off after Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut. SoftBank Group, an OpenAI backer, led the slide.

The benchmark has now shed 12.38% over a month, though it remains 11.46% higher year to date. SoftBank, down more than 11%, and Japanese chip stocks took the hardest hits.

Why Is Anthropic’s Listing Hitting Tokyo So Hard?

Anthropic, the AI startup behind Claude, debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday with an $81 billion offering, AP reported.

Meanwhile, Nvidia (NVDA) slid 2.9% overnight and the Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2%.

SoftBank has put $64.6 billion into OpenAI, Anthropic’s rival, which ties its shares closely to AI sentiment.

SoftBank shed 30% in October and has lost 31% in November so far. At 10:25 a.m. in Tokyo, it was down 11.99%.

CNBC attributes the sell-off to doubts over whether AI infrastructure spending will pay off. However, OpenAI cut its funding target by $10 billion this month, and some investors waited for Anthropic’s listing price first.

Does the Nikkei 225 Sell-Off Stop at SoftBank?

It does not. Chip equipment makers Tokyo Electron and Lasertec shed 7.19% and 6.75%, and chipmaker Renesas Electronics gave up 6.71%.

The losses spread to South Korea. Samsung Electronics lost 4.7% and SK Hynix 6%, both Nvidia suppliers. The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi) fell 3.66%.

The Nikkei closed Thursday at 59,443.99 and has lost 7.13% over five days and 13.10% over three months. In contrast, it is still up 15.73% over one year, per TradingView.

The mood was different when Anthropic filed to list. On Oct. 27, the Nikkei rose 1.7% and SoftBank gained 5%, Fortune reported.

If losses hold, SoftBank faces its biggest one-day drop in over two years, CNBC reported. Japanese and South Korean chipmakers both sit in the AI hardware chain. Therefore, a weak Nasdaq session reaches their shares by the next Asian open.

By Courtney Rozen 
   WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White ‌House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking ‌and national security systems. 
   The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face ​mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights. 
   The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal ‌is the administration's first major ⁠personnel move since the outages. 
   Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer ⁠Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source. 
   "The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition ​of anonymity. 
   Cairncross ​said  in a statement on Thursday night it ​was the "honor of a lifetime ‌to serve" in Trump's administration. 
   The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections. 
   The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were ‌separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical ​changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored ​attack. 
   Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri ​on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should ‌brief lawmakers on the outages so ​they can “share with ​the American people what’s happening here.” 
   Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need ​to be confirmed by ‌the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in ​January. 
   (Reporting by Courtney Rozen and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by ​Caitlin Webber, John Mair and Lincoln Feast.) 
This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/white-house-national-cyber-director-222714781.html

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face ​mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.

The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal ‌is the administration's first major ⁠personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer ⁠Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.

"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition ​of anonymity.

Cairncross ​said in a statement on Thursday night it ​was the "honor of a lifetime ‌to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.

The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were ‌separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical ​changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored ​attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri ​on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should ‌brief lawmakers on the outages so ​they can “share with ​the American people what’s happening here.”

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need ​to be confirmed by ‌the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in ​January.

title: DOJ ditches lawsuit that sought to pause certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate election
description:
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in early 2026. (Photo by Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Attorneys representing the U.S. Department of Justice told the federal 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday that they are no longer pursuing a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections over its handling of the state’s U.S. Senate election.
In a new filing, attorneys for the federal agency said “this case has become moot,” a statement signaling they will not oppose the state certifying Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as the winner of the election.
On Wednesday, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher said she intends to certify the election, including Peltola’s victory over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, next week.
According to preliminary results through Wednesday, Peltola’s margin over Sullivan is greater than the number of first-choice votes cast for Sullivan and all other candidates combined. When seated in Congress, she will join a 56-person Democratic Senate majority elected amid a nationwide surge of support for Democratic candidates.
Last month, the federal government, at the urging of President Donald Trump, sued the state and asked a federal judge to issue an order that would preclude elections officials from certifying Peltola as the election winner while it investigated whether the presence of independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan confused Alaska voters.
Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins


U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit, saying the federal government lacked standing, but the Department of Justice appealed to the 9th Circuit.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the national organization Common Cause, arguing on the appeal, asked the appellate court to issue a summary order upholding Gleason’s decision and asked the appellate judges to punish the federal attorneys that filed the case.
“The legal theory advanced by the United States here is embarrassing and indefensible,” wrote attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union, which represented the two groups. “The Court should summarily affirm and then order the attorneys for the United States to explain why they or their client should not be sanctioned for pursuing a frivolous appeal.”
On Thursday, the federal government responded, saying that instead of summarily upholding Gleason’s decision, the appeals court should vacate it, erasing it from the books entirely, because it is now moot.
Alaskans have now voted, the federal government said, and ballots for Dan J. Sullivan are mixed with other ballots, making it impossible to determine who voted for Dan J. Sullivan.
“The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,” the federal attorneys wrote.
In late October, the New York Times reported that Dan J. Sullivan had been recruited by Democratic campaigners who sought to spoil the re-election campaign of Sen. Dan Sullivan. 
“The purpose of this lawsuit,” federal attorneys wrote, “was always to make sure that voters had the opportunity to cast a vote accurately reflecting their choice of candidate, notwithstanding the confusion caused (and intended to be caused) by Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign, egged on by Peltola’s.”
While the civil lawsuit is winding down, a separate criminal investigation is continuing. The Anchorage Daily News reported on Wednesday that both the Alaska Bureau of Investigation and FBI are continuing to investigate whether any laws were violated by Dan J. Sullivan’s recruitment as a candidate.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This article originally appeared on Alaska Beacon at https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/11/19/doj-abandons-lawsuit-that-sought-to-pause-certification-of-alaskas-us-senate-election/

title: California State Bar opens investigation into former White House press secretary
description:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, right, joins President Trump as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images)
The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia, who faced scrutiny during her brief stint as White House press secretary for calling herself a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam. 
The probe, which was made public on Thursday, comes in response to a complaint submitted last month by the nonprofit watchdog Campaign for Accountability alleging that Zacharia may have violated California law by touting herself as lawyer.
While Zacharia, a Huntington Beach native, received a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, she did not pass the bar exam in California or any other state. Yet, since at least early 2025 she has described herself as a lawyer on national television and in podcasts, including on “The Greg Kelly Show” and CNN, and has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 appearances on Fox News, according to the complaint.
“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie. In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” the organization’s executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release last month.
Read more: Questions swirl about new White House press secretary's resume
The watchdog’s complaint alleges Zacharia claimed to have served as “outside counsel” to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and previously listed herself on LinkedIn as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a nonprofit.
A spokesperson for Zacharia denied that she had violated any laws in a text message to The Times, calling the accusations “baseless.”
“This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing,” the spokesperson said.
Under California state law a person presenting themselves as being entitled to practice law without an active state bar license could be charged with a misdemeanor and face up to a year in county jail and a $1,000 fine.
Read more: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start
Zacharia addressed the scrutiny last month in an interview with conservative outlet Human Events, saying she had been preparing to take the bar exam in California shortly after getting married and was busy preparing for a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.
“I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I’d been long distance from for at least a year,” Zacharia told the outlet, adding that the results of the exam were “somewhat inconsequential” because she knew she would not need the credential in China.
She said she had consulted several legal experts to ensure the title of lawyer was accurate when offering legal analysis and “they said absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer,” she told the outlet.
Zacharia added that it was “unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy.”
Times staff writer Clara Harter contributed to this report.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

title: Bitcoin Falls Below $62k Amid $528M in Liquidations
description: Following the Anthropic IPO, BTC has logged another multi-month low.
fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC) lost support at $62,000 on Friday, briefly falling below $61,500 for the first time since July.  

  • According to TradingView, BTC fell to just $61,381 at 21:32 UTC, before resurging back to $62,048 at writing time.
  • Data from CoinGlass confirms that another $528M in liquidations has occurred across the crypto market in the last 24 hours, including $169M of liquidations for BTC alone. 
  • Roughly 80% of the value liquidated came from longs. Over 113,000 traders were liquidated in total. 
  • Strategy (MSTR) followed suit, falling even further to $85.72 after hours, close to -5% on the day. The bitcoin juggernaut now trades for less than the total BTC on its balance sheet, with a self-reported “mNAV” of 0.97X.
  • The price dump follows the highly anticipated Anthropic (ANT) IPO earlier today – one of the largest public offerings in world history.
  • The Anthropic deal raised $81.3 billion for $83 per share. Following Thursday’s close, ANT traded for $91.81 after hours, and boasted a market capitalization $1.272 trillion – roughly equal to Bitcoin.

The post Bitcoin Falls Below $62k Amid $528M in Liquidations appeared first on CryptoPotato.

title: AI is Worsening Inflation and Making Things More Expensive, IMF Warns
description:
IMF chief Georgieva says AI demand is fueling global inflation, as Wall Street ranks AI its top financial risk.
The post AI is Worsening Inflation and Making Things More Expensive, IMF Warns appeared first on BeInCrypto.
fullContent:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is now holding up the world economy. On Thursday, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said it is also making the world more expensive.

Kristalina Georgieva told Asia-Pacific leaders in Shenzhen, China, that AI demand and the oil shock will lift global inflation to 4.7%.

Her solution is tighter money, meaning costlier loans for families, companies, and governments.

How AI Became an Inflation Problem

Tech giants are racing to build data centers, buying chips and power in huge volumes. That spending is lifting growth.

Georgieva said 2026 is the first year AI has had a real impact on global growth. It helped offset the oil shock from turmoil in the Middle East.

The catch is timing. The money goes out now, and the benefits come later, Georgieva warned in October.

“Both the energy supply shock and the AI demand shock are pushing global inflation up to 4.7% this year. This calls for tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Bond yields in many rich countries are at multi-decade highs, she added. In the US, the 10-year Treasury yield, which guides mortgage rates, sat near 5.1% as of this writing.

Why Wall Street Fears the Thing Driving Growth

The New York Fed asked 23 professionals at banks, dealers, and funds to name the biggest risks to US finance. Some 87% picked AI, up from 50% in the spring.

“Nearly 90% of respondents cited AI as the biggest risk to U.S. financial stability over the next 12-18 months… risk asset correction and higher long-term rates rounded out the top three,” noted Liz Ann Sonders, Chief Investment Strategist at Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The boom runs on debt. Borrowing for computing power passed $680 billion by October, the Fed’s report showed.

If AI profits disappoint, Georgieva said in October, that debt and foreign holdings of US stocks could spread a global shock.

The pain is uneven. Energy importers are struggling, she said, while energy exporters tied to AI are thriving.

Oil, she said, is a passing shock. AI is not.

“And while the energy shock will eventually dissipate, AI is forever the most significant factor for medium-term competitiveness, productivity, and growth.”

Traders are now placing bets on a Fed hike in December. That meeting will show whether the Fed treats AI demand as a reason to raise rates again.
