The post My Wallet Introduces 1:1 Cross-Chain Stablecoin Swaps After Being Listed First on WalletConnect appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
November 19th, 2026 – Dubai, United Arab Emirates

My Wallet users can now receive a different stablecoin on another blockchain at a fixed 1:1 token rate on eligible routes, with no spread, slippage or swap fee charged by the wallet

My Wallet, a self-custodial, open-source crypto wallet serving more than 10 million users, has launched 1:1 swaps for USDT, USDC, USDe and USDS across supported blockchains. On eligible routes, users can switch both stablecoins and networks within a single in-app flow, with the amount they will receive fixed before confirmation. 

The launch follows My Wallet’s listing at the top of WalletConnect’s WalletGuide. The wallet is also WalletConnect Certified and connects users to more than 80,000 compatible apps.

Simplifying Stablecoin Transfers Across Blockchains

According to research published in October 2026 by Coinbase and The Block Pro Research, organic stablecoin transfer volume exceeded $400 million per hour during Q3 2026. Yet stablecoins operate across multiple blockchains and token issuers, creating friction when users need a specific token on a specific network. Even when funds arrive on the right network, users may still hold the wrong stablecoin for a payment, trade or application.

My Wallet addresses this through its in-app swap aggregator, powered by LayerZero, NEAR Intents, and other bridges resulting in the best rate. On eligible stablecoin routes, the aggregator offers a fixed 1:1 token rate, with no exchange-rate spread, slippage or My Wallet swap commission. My Wallet is the first among major crypto wallets to offer 1:1 swaps between different stablecoins across blockchains in a single in-app flow.

How the 1:1 Stablecoin Swaps Work

The fixed 1:1 rate can apply whether users switch to a different stablecoin or move the same token to another blockchain. On a supported cross-chain USDT-to-USDC route, for example, a user sending 10,000 USDT receives exactly 10,000 USDC. The same rate applies when the token stays the same: a supported transfer of 10,000 USDT from Ethereum to TRON delivers exactly 10,000 USDT on TRON.

The 1:1 option is available for swaps above $30 on supported routes. There is no exchange-rate spread, slippage or My Wallet swap commission. Applicable blockchain network fees are paid separately, and the exact destination token amount is shown before confirmation. Other routes may have different rates and fees.

“Stablecoins are supposed to make moving money simpler, but users still have to think about which token they hold and which blockchain it’s on,” said Alexander Zinchuk, founder of My Wallet. “We’re removing that friction. If you hold USDT and need USDC on another network, you should be able to make that change in one step, know exactly how many tokens you’ll receive, and not pay an additional swap commission to your wallet.”

Native Bitcoin and Gasless EVM Transfers

The stablecoin launch follows the introduction of native Bitcoin support in My Wallet. Users can hold, send, receive and swap BTC alongside assets on Ethereum, Solana, TON and other networks, as well as buy Bitcoin with a bank card or sell it for fiat through MoonPay.

My Wallet now supports gasless transfers on Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Arbitrum and Optimism, adding to the existing support on Solana and TON. For these EVM transfers, the network fee is deducted from the tokens being sent, so users do not need to acquire a separate native token for gas. Supported assets are USDC on all five EVM networks, USDT on Ethereum and BNB Chain, bridged USDT on Base and Optimism, and USDT0 on Arbitrum. There is no minimum transfer amount or daily limit on the number of transactions.

Together, these innovative features advance My Wallet’s broader “All You Need to Enjoy Crypto” vision, combining asset management, seamless trading, and ease of use into one self-custodial app.

The new features are already available in My Wallet. Swap availability is subject to the selected assets, networks and routes.

About My Wallet

My Wallet is a self-custodial, open-source multichain wallet for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Hyperliquid, TON, TRON, BNB, Base, Robinhood, Monad, Arbitrum, Polygon, and more. Founded in 2022, My Wallet serves over 10 million users across mobile, desktop, web and its Telegram Mini App. The wallet has been audited by CertiK and ranks among the top-5 wallets on CertiK’s Wallet Leaderboard.

My Wallet is WalletConnect Certified and currently listed 1st in WalletConnect’s WalletGuide, connecting users to more than 80,000 compatible apps.

Staking inside My Wallet is powered by Stakee, its own staking protocol, ranked among the top-2 TON DeFi protocols by TVL on DefiLlama.

For more details, users can visit mywallet.io and try My Wallet at mywallet.io/get.

title: LIVE – Bitcoin Price, Gold and Oil Fall: Should the US Repeat Its $2.2T 2020 Rescue?
description:
Bitcoin price, gold and oil fall as hawkish Fed minutes fuel rate hike fears. Should Washington repeat its $2.2T rescue from 2020?
The post LIVE – Bitcoin Price, Gold and Oil Fall: Should the US Repeat Its $2.2T 2020 Rescue? appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

Almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

Bitcoin Price Under Pressure as the Fed Flags Leverage Risks

Bitcoin (BTC)
24h7d30d1yAll time

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

The risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets quickly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

The Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Remember March 2020? The Fed Cut Rates to Zero and Washington Spent $2.2T

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

Should Washington Pull Off Another $2.2T Rescue?

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

title: Ant, DBS Use Blockchain Cash to Buy Tokenized Funds
description:
Summary Cash stays locked until fund tokens move Pilot ran under Singapore’s MAS-led BLOOM initiative Builds on DBS-Ant Treasury Tokens […]
The post Ant, DBS Use Blockchain Cash to Buy Tokenized Funds appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Summary

  • Cash stays locked until fund tokens move
  • Pilot ran under Singapore’s MAS-led BLOOM initiative
  • Builds on DBS-Ant Treasury Tokens from 2024
  • Values, timings and fees remain undisclosed

Ant International announced the Whale Orchestration Protocol, which connects tokenized deposits and money market funds through its WhaleRTP wholesale settlement platform, and published a whitepaper explaining how the link works.

The deposit rail already existed. The fund leg is new

Ant and DBS have been building toward this since August 2024, when DBS launched a Treasury Tokens pilot with Ant International for round-the-clock treasury and liquidity management. Those tokens run on DBS’s permissioned, EVM-compatible blockchain, which is wired into the bank’s core payments engine and connected to Ant’s Whale treasury platform. The original aim was internal: moving Ant’s own money between its entities in seconds rather than days.

The new pilot points that rail outward. The partners completed transactions linking DBS Treasury Tokens with Franklin Templeton’s tokenized money market fund solutions. The cash leg is a bank deposit token; the asset leg is a fund unit recorded on a separate system.

The work sits under BLOOM, an initiative the Monetary Authority of Singapore launched in October 2025 to support settlement in tokenized bank liabilities and well-regulated stablecoins. Corporate treasury management is one of its named wholesale use cases, and Ant International co-leads BLOOM’s work on programmable compliance controls.

The two assets carry different legal claims. A tokenized deposit is a claim on DBS; a tokenized fund unit is an interest in a fund. Recording both on blockchains gives them a common format but leaves them on separate ledgers, and that separation is the problem the protocol sets out to solve.

A lien replaces “you go first”

Securities markets handle this with delivery versus payment, or DvP. BIS research describes it as tying delivery to payment so that neither happens without the other. That removes principal risk: paying and never receiving the asset, or delivering it and never being paid.

Inside one ledger, DvP can run as a single transaction. Across two, something has to hold one side still while the other moves. The whitepaper’s answer is a lien on the deposit tokens. The owner keeps legal ownership, but the cash can’t be spent elsewhere while it is committed to the trade. Once the fund side’s issuance or cancellation of tokens is verified, the payment is released.

The protocol itself validates and relays transaction states between the two systems. The paper describes it as neither an asset bridge nor a settlement ledger: deposit tokens stay on DBS’s chain, fund units stay with the fund, and nothing is wrapped into a third token. The fund keeps its own eligibility, compliance, transfer-agency and operational controls.

For a treasury, that means no new bridged asset to hold or value. The design relies instead on each ledger reporting its state accurately and on the protocol reading it correctly.

Following $1 million in and out of a fund

Take a treasury with $1 million it won’t need for several weeks. It wants to earn money market yield on the balance and recover the cash before its next supplier payment run. The amount is illustrative, not a figure from the pilot.

Going in: subscription

  1. Lock. $1 million of the treasury’s DBS Treasury Tokens goes under lien. The treasury still owns it.
  2. Issue. After its own checks, the fund issues units to the treasury as tokens.
  3. Release. The protocol confirms issuance, and the locked cash is paid to the fund.

Coming out: redemption

  1. Lock. The cash that will pay the redemption goes under lien.
  2. Cancel. The fund cancels the treasury’s fund tokens.
  3. Release. Cancellation is confirmed, and proceeds arrive as DBS Treasury Tokens.

Based on the workflow in the partners’ whitepaper.

The interval that counts is the one between instruction and confirmation. During it, the $1 million still belongs to the treasury but can’t cover payroll or a supplier invoice. A shorter window means less cash sitting frozen, yet the public material gives no figure for how long that window lasted in the pilot.

The redemption leg also ends somewhere specific: a DBS Treasury Token balance. Whether that’s the end of the journey depends on whom the treasury needs to pay next.

Settlement liquidity isn’t spending liquidity

Treasurers deal with three kinds of liquidity. Investment liquidity is the ability to exit a holding on the fund’s terms. Settlement liquidity is having cash and assets ready at the moment of exchange. Operational liquidity is having usable money in the right account when a payment falls due.

The pilot addresses the second. It makes the swap itself safer and removes the need for either side to trust the other with the first move. The other two kinds of liquidity are left where they were.

Investment liquidity still depends on the fund. Eligibility approval, dealing cut-offs and the price at which units are issued or cancelled are set by the fund’s terms, and those steps come before the final exchange. A treasury that misses a dealing window gains nothing from a faster swap at the end.

Operational liquidity depends on where the proceeds land. A DBS Treasury Token balance can pay a counterparty on the same network. A supplier that banks elsewhere, or invoices in another currency, needs a further transfer or conversion, which the pilot material leaves out. Coindoo’s coverage of the JPMorgan-DBS tokenized-dollar service deals with that next step: moving tokenized dollars between two banks’ networks around the clock.

READ MORE:

Tether’s Payments Bet Goes Beyond Sending USDT

What the pilot hasn’t shown

The announcement leaves out transaction values, measured completion times, fees, which customers can use the service and the exact fund share class. The pilot runs between regulated institutions, and nothing in the material points to purchases through public crypto wallets.

Three figures would show whether the design helps a working treasury: how long a typical lien stays in place, how often instructions fail or need correcting, and how quickly redemption proceeds can settle a payment outside the DBS network. The last of those decides whether a fund holding can stand in for cash on a payment day.

title: Tether’s Payments Bet Goes Beyond Sending USDT
description:
Key takeaways Tether and Further added roughly $10 million MetaComp’s router can bypass stablecoins entirely 24-hour settlement claim lacks a […]
The post Tether’s Payments Bet Goes Beyond Sending USDT appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key takeaways

  • Tether and Further added roughly $10 million
  • MetaComp’s router can bypass stablecoins entirely
  • 24-hour settlement claim lacks a stated endpoint
  • Conversion costs can outweigh blockchain fees

MetaComp disclosed the funding in an announcement that extends its Pre-A round to about $45 million.

What Tether and Further are paying for

The new money builds on a $35 million Pre-A and Pre-A+ round that MetaComp completed in March, backed by investors including Alibaba, Sky9 Capital and Noah. The release does not say how the latest $10 million splits between its two investors.

Further Asset Management is an Abu Dhabi-based firm that invests in financial infrastructure and digital assets. Managing partner Faisal Al Hammadi said MetaComp fits its focus on the infrastructure behind institutional adoption.

Tether’s stated reasons are more specific. CEO Paolo Ardoino pointed to the payment corridors linking Asia, the Middle East and Africa, saying “regulated stablecoin infrastructure can change that.” He described those corridors as places where Tether sees room for USDT and its gold-backed XAUT token. The company frames the investment as part of building infrastructure in emerging markets, where faster and cheaper settlement matters most. That fits the broader push of stablecoins into cross-border payments.

MetaComp says the capital will go to licenses, compliance and additional payment channels in priority markets. Singapore’s MAS directory lists it as a Major Payment Institution licensed for cross-border money transfer and digital payment token services. That license covers its Singapore activity, not every market where a supplier might be paid, which helps explain why licenses top the spending list. The company says it already connects with more than 60 financial institutions and 170 payment service providers and supports 60 currencies.

A router that doesn’t have to pick USDT

The product at the center of the deal is StableX. Its product page says an intelligent routing engine chooses between stablecoin and US dollar rails based on cost, speed and settlement certainty, and it names USDT and USDC among the supported tokens. A payment through MetaComp can therefore travel as USDT, as USDC or as a conventional dollar transfer, without the customer holding a crypto wallet.

That makes Tether’s return harder to read than the headline figure suggests. Whenever the engine picks USDC or a bank rail, Tether’s token never moves. Whatever the route, the investment does buy a stake in a licensed firm that controls the parts of a payment USDT cannot handle alone: the bank connections, the currency conversion and the compliance checks, in corridors Tether has named as priorities.

MetaComp’s volume figure does not show how often USDT wins. The company reports more than $1 billion in monthly processing volume as of October 30, but it also runs wealth products and reports more than $600 million in assets under management. The release gives no breakdown by product, payment rail or stablecoin, so USDT’s share of that billion is not public.

Where each side starts and finishes also shapes whether USDT helps. A sender that already holds USDT skips a purchase, and a supplier willing to keep stablecoins skips a bank payout. A supplier that wants local currency in its bank account needs both ends handled. Coindoo’s guide to crypto payments covers how each of those legs works.

Where a stablecoin payment can stall

When a business pays an overseas supplier in local currency, the token transfer is only the middle of five stages, and each stage has its own sources of delay and cost.

1. Funding

Can delay: wire timing at the sender’s bank, onboarding and identity review

Can cost: outgoing bank fees

2. Fiat to stablecoin

Can delay: sanctions and transaction screening

Can cost: conversion spread or fee

3. On-chain transfer

Can delay: network confirmations, Travel Rule data exchange between providers

Can cost: network fee, usually the smallest item

4. Local conversion

Can delay: sourcing liquidity in less-traded currencies

Can cost: spread against the market rate

5. Bank payout

Can delay: local banking hours, cut-off times, receiving-bank checks

Can cost: payout and receiving-bank fees

Only the third stage runs purely on a blockchain. The other four depend on banks, liquidity providers and compliance teams, the same areas MetaComp says the new funding will strengthen.

The 24-hour claim has no stated finish line

According to the release, MetaComp’s hybrid model cuts settlement from 2–7 days to within 24 hours on corridors connecting Asia, the Middle East and Africa. It does not say when that clock starts or stops: when the receiving provider gets the tokens, when local conversion completes or when the supplier’s bank credits the account. It also does not say which conventional route the 2–7 day baseline describes.

No per-corridor results are published, and the release does not say how it counts payments held for extra review or sent over a weekend. StableX advertises round-the-clock foreign exchange, but the final credit still depends on the receiving country’s payment system, and not all of those run around the clock.

READ MORE:

Crypto Traders Can Get 3x Equity Exposure Through Spot Tokens

On a $10,000 transfer, the chain fee is the small number

A BIS working paper published on October 19 by Wenxin Du, Catherine Huang and David Scharfstein compares bank, fintech and stablecoin routes. The authors find that converting between fiat and stablecoins runs through exchanges and other intermediaries whose trading, conversion and withdrawal fees can substantially raise the total cost. They also find liquidity between dollar stablecoins and non-US currencies is generally very thin. Where stablecoins offered better exchange rates on some transfers into emerging markets, the paper attributes the gap to capital controls rather than to the technology. The paper does not assess MetaComp.

It does give benchmarks for the alternatives. In a small sample, bank wires carried exchange-rate markups of roughly 2% to 4.7% before explicit wire fees. Fintech money transfer operators charged a median of about $40 to $60 to send $10,000 from the US into developed-market currencies. In both cases, the currency conversion drives the cost, not the transfer itself.

The same holds inside a stablecoin route. On a hypothetical $10,000 payment, a 0.50% conversion spread costs $50. Cutting the network fee from $5 to $1 saves $4, while trimming that spread to 0.20% saves $30. These are illustrative inputs, not MetaComp’s prices.

MetaComp labels the rates it displays as indicative and non-binding, subject to market conditions at execution. The figure that matters is the firm quote a customer accepts, measured as the amount debited against the amount the supplier receives, using the same reference rate for every route being compared.

Tether has bought into the parts of a payment that USDT cannot complete on its own: the licenses, bank links and currency conversion at each end. MetaComp has not disclosed how often its own router decides USDT is the best way through. That number would say more about the value of Tether’s stake than the size of the check.

Why Blue-Chip NFTs Like Lil Pudgys and Azuki Are Trending While Crypto Crashes
description:
A basket of blue-chip NFTs is climbing while the tokens around it bleed. CoinGecko’s trending NFT data showed Lil Pudgys up 9.08% on the day, Azuki up 8.06%, CryptoPunks up
The post Why Blue-Chip NFTs Like Lil Pudgys and Azuki Are Trending While Crypto Crashes appeared first on NFT Plazas.
fullContent:
A basket of blue-chip NFTs is climbing while the tokens around it bleed. CoinGecko’s trending NFT data showed Lil Pudgys up 9.08% on the day, Azuki up 8.06%, CryptoPunks up 4.84%, Pudgy Penguins up 4.14% and Mutant Ape Yacht Club (MAYC) up 3.87% in 24-hour floor price.

The backdrop could hardly be worse. Bitcoin slipped below $65,000 and Ether hovered near $1,800 on Wednesday, after a week in which Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan said BTC lost 12% and ETH 14% on a U.S. rate shock. CoinGecko’s Fear & Greed gauge reads Extreme Fear. Yet the oldest, most recognizable NFT collections are quietly moving the other way.

Five blue chips up, three majors down

All five trending collections gained in the same 24 hours that BTC and ETH fell, according to CoinGecko’s trending feed earlier Wednesday. The latest CoinGecko readings show those daily moves cooling to low single digits, with floors still near the levels below.

Collection 24h floor change (trending feed) Latest floor (ETH) Latest floor (USD, approx.) 24h sales
Lil Pudgys +9.08% 0.22 $397 11
Azuki +8.06% 0.48 $869 10
CryptoPunks +4.84% 28.24 $51,140 —
Pudgy Penguins +4.14% 2.39 $4,330 11
MAYC +3.87% 0.88 $1,587 24

On the token side, Bitcoin fell about 1% to $64,694 and Ether about 1.3% to roughly $1,808, per CoinGecko-based reports. Solana bounced around 3% on the day to near $75, but that follows a week in which SOL, like ETH, lost about 22%. Total crypto market value sits near $2.28 trillion.

The NFT sector is far smaller. CoinGecko puts global NFT market cap at about $1.21 billion, with only $1.42 million in 24-hour volume.

Bitcoin (BTC) Price Performance on Nov 18, 2026 (Source: CoinGecko)

Why the basket is breaking from tokens

Three forces explain most of the split: thin order books, ETH-priced floors and a rotation toward established brands.

Thin books move fast. Pudgy Penguins logged 11 sales in 24 hours and Azuki just 10. When sellers pull listings instead of dumping into a falling market, a handful of buyers can lift the cheapest ask several percent. Fungible tokens, by contrast, trade billions a day and absorb every macro headline instantly.

Floors are quoted in ETH. A floor that rises in ETH while ETH drops is partly a currency effect. Sellers who think in dollars raise their ETH asks to defend value, and buyers holding ETH find blue chips cheap in their own unit. Either way, the floor ticks up even when demand barely changes.

Money is rotating into names with history. CryptoSlam data reported by TokenPost shows weekly NFT sales rose 6.13% to $35.11 million in the week to November 17, even as transactions fell 6%. CryptoPunks sales jumped 252% to $1.21 million in that window. Fewer trades, bigger tickets and concentration in marquee collections point to collectors buying quality, not chasing mints.

The IP plays have real-world news

The leaders of this move are brands that sell things off-chain, and each has a fresh headline.

Pudgy Penguins and Lil Pudgys. A PSA 10 Pudgy Penguins Vibes card is listed in eBay-owned Goldin’s Fall TCG Elite Auction, beside Pokémon lots, with extended bidding from November 30. Pudgy products also reached 330 Kung Fu Tea locations this month, adding to plush lines in roughly 2,000 Walmart and 1,800-plus Target stores. Pudgy NFT sales rose 71% week on week to $588,280 in the period to November 14, while the wider NFT market slipped. Lil Pudgys, a 22,222-piece companion set to the 8,888 originals, offers the cheapest entry into that brand at about 0.22 ETH, which helps explain why it led the basket.

The contrast with the brand’s token is stark. PENGU fell nearly 21% in seven days to about $0.005. Holders appear to prefer the NFT, which carries IP licensing upside, over a token whose terms say it has no claim on company revenue.

Azuki. Chiru Labs now calls Azuki an IP company built around a trading card game and a manga. Its second card set, Fractured Domains (AZK-02), is due in stores on November 20, giving traders a dated catalyst two days out.

CryptoPunks and MAYC. Punks remain the sector’s reserve asset, holding about 42% of NFT market-cap dominance on CoinGecko. MAYC, at under 1 ETH, is the cheapest route into the Yuga Labs ape ecosystem and recorded the most sales of the five, at 24.

Why the rally may not stick

The same thin liquidity that lifts floors can sink them just as quickly. With the whole NFT market trading about $1.42 million in 24 hours, a single motivated seller could erase a day’s gains.

The dollar math is also less impressive than the ETH math. A 4% floor gain on CryptoPunks roughly offsets one day of ETH weakness; it does not undo ETH’s 14% slide last week. In USD terms, most of these collections remain far below their 2021–22 peaks; Azuki once floored near 30 ETH.

Macro risk has not cleared. Hougan tied last week’s sell-off to a hotter-than-expected U.S. CPI print, a jump in two-year Treasury yields and about $2 billion in weekend leveraged liquidations, and analysts now point to the December Fed decision as the next test. Pudgy’s ecosystem faces its own friction too: the Abstract chain it backed is set to shut down on December 15.

What to watch next

The next two weeks will show whether blue chips are a refuge or just a pocket of illiquidity. Four markers matter:

  • November 20: Azuki’s Fractured Domains card set lands in stores; watch whether the floor holds after the event.
  • November 30: extended bidding opens on the Pudgy Penguins card at Goldin, a test of crossover demand from traditional collectors.
  • ETH near $1,750: Tuesday’s intraday low. A break lower would pressure ETH-priced floors from both sides.
  • Weekly CryptoSlam sales: a second week of rising dollar volume with concentration in blue chips would confirm rotation rather than noise.

For now, the signal is narrow but clear. In a market gripped by fear, collectors are paying up for NFTs with brands, products and years of history, not for the tokens that trade beside them.

NGINX2Root: Five nginx Flaws, Led by CVE-2026-123007. How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch Now
description: Executive Summary NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker […]
fullContent:
Executive Summary

NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw. Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault.

HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch.

F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint, the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port.

In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business:

  • Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker.
  • A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position.
  • Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections.

Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root.

NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration:

The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach.

Why NGINX2Root Is Also an Application Security Problem 

NGINX2Root is an infrastructure flaw, but its impact lands on the applications behind nginx. Where nginx terminates TLS and proxies requests, every login, API call, and session cookie bound for those applications passes through the worker process in clear text. An attacker running code in that worker sits between users and the applications they trust: 

  • Credentials and tokens become reusable. Passwords, session cookies, API keys, and bearer tokens read from the worker can be replayed directly against the applications and APIs behind the proxy, where they look like legitimate user traffic. 
  • Trust placed in the proxy becomes the attacker’s. Backend services, internal APIs, and admin interfaces are often reachable only from the proxy. Applications that accept identity or client details from headers the proxy sets, such as X-Forwarded-For or user headers added after single sign-on, trust whatever the compromised proxy sends. 
  • Application traffic can be altered in transit. Requests and responses pass through the worker, so the attacker is positioned to change what users receive and what the backend processes, with no change to application code. 
  • One proxy, many applications. A shared reverse proxy or Kubernetes ingress controller often fronts dozens of applications owned by different teams. A worker crash takes all of them offline at once. 

For application security teams, the scoping question is not only which hosts run a vulnerable nginx build, but which applications and APIs depend on them, what data those applications handle, and who owns them. 

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself.

F5 notes that it did not evaluate versions past End of Technical Support. F5 also lists BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, and F5OS as not vulnerable in its advisory.

The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on.

nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o — ‘–with-http_v2_module’

sudo nginx -T 2>&1 | sed ‘s/#.*//’ | grep -nE ‘listen[[:space:]].*http2|^[[:space:]]*http2[[:space:]]+on[[:space:]]*;’

Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet.

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’

nginx also ships inside other software. Status as of November 18, 2026:

Three cautions when scoping:

  • Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory.
  • Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly.
  • Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network.

Exploitation Status

As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild.

Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps.

The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors.

These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow.

What to Do Now

Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026.

Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007.

Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart.

If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive, CERT-EU’s advisory, and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch.

Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams

Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response:

  • Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency.
  • Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe.
  • Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back.
  • Map each nginx instance to the applications and APIs behind it. A host inventory shows where a vulnerable build is installed; it does not show which applications, owners, and data depend on it. Use that mapping to set priority and to notify application owners, not to close findings. 
  • Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends.
  • Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance.
  • Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet.

How Qualys Can Help

Inventory nginx Installations with Qualys CSAM

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too.

Assets With nginx in the Affected Range

Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected NGINX Open Source installations on the stable, mainline, and older branches for further assessment. It uses two ranges because 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 are affected even though they are higher than the fixed 1.30.7.

software:(name:”nginx” AND ( (version>=1.9.5 AND version<1.30.7) OR (version>=1.31.0 AND version<1.31.9) ))

Detect NGINX2Root at Disclosure with Qualys InstaScan 

NGINX2Root will not be patched everywhere at once. On November 18, F5 shipped NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, fixed NGINX Plus 37.x builds, and updated releases of NGINX Ingress Controller and NGINX Gateway Fabric, and the official Docker image now carries fixed tags. Older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, and Ubuntu and Debian still list their stable nginx packages as vulnerable. n, powered by Agent Insta, keeps detection from waiting on any of those schedules. It checks every new vendor advisory against the software inventory Qualys already has for your assets, whether that inventory came from Qualys Cloud Agents, Qualys scanners, or third-party tools you have connected.   

For assets in your InstaScan scope, vulnerable nginx installations show up as CVE-2026-123007 findings in Qualys ETM, typically within minutes of the advisory, with no scan to schedule. That gives your team owners and deadlines to work with before the VMDR detection QIDs below are released. Because InstaScan matches on the installed nginx version, it cannot see whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a distribution has backported the fix. Use the checks in Are You Affected? to decide which findings to work first, and close them only on the evidence described above.  

Where to find InstaScan findings. CVE-2026-123007 findings land in Qualys ETM under Risk Management → Findings → InstaScan, a tab that holds only the last 48 hours or so of InstaScan detections. After that they move to the Vulnerabilities tab. When a Cloud Agent or scanner later detects the same CVE on the same asset, the two detections are merged into one record rather than duplicated. To pull InstaScan findings back up in the Vulnerabilities tab, search for finding.isInstaScan: TRUE, click the InstaScan summary card, or look for the InstaScan badge in the Sources column. 

Identify Applications Potentially Impacted by NGINX2Root with Qualys TotalAppSec 

CSAM and VMDR show where vulnerable nginx is installed. TotalAppSec answers the question application security teams need answered next: which web applications and APIs are served through it, and who owns them. 

Discover the full application attack surface. TotalAppSec continuously discovers web applications and APIs across internet-facing and internal environments, on premises and in the cloud, including unknown, forgotten, shadow, and rogue applications. It builds a unified inventory by integrating with Qualys EASM and CSAM and with API sources such as Postman and MuleSoft.

title: Variational Hits $1.5B Valuation in $110M Round to Take on Robinhood and IBKR
description:
Crypto trading startup Variational raised $110 million at a $1.5 billion valuation in the Series B round to compete with brokerages like Robinhood Markets Inc. and Interactive Brokers LLC. 
The financing round was led by Bain Capital Crypto, an early-stage crypto-native fund, where Stefan Cohen is a partner.  Other participants included Dragonfly Capital, HSG and Peak XV. 
“They’re [Variational] basically plugging into all of these off-chain liquidity sources and innovating on this broker model that they’ve established,” said Stefan Cohen.
 Crypto Startup with Traditional Finance Ambitions 
Variational is a derivatives trading protocol registered in the Cayman Islands that lets users trade swaps and perpetuals for both crypto and traditional assets, including stocks, commodities and pre-IPO equities. 
The company reports over 100,000 accounts and more than $475 billion in trading volume processed since launching the trading platform in 2025. 
Variational operates on a brokerage model, routing trades to and from crypto protocols and centralised trading venues, with over half of the platform's daily volume now on traditional markets. 
Unlike other on-chain trading platforms, Variational aggregates liquidity from both traditional and on-chain markets, making this dual approach integral to its strategy.
“I think there’s a place for both of us in the ecosystem, especially because again, we’re building just a very different type of product for TradFi trading,” said Variational chief executive officer Lucas Schuermann. 
While the platform is often viewed as a Hyperliquid rival, Schuermann said they're setting their sights on brokerages like Robinhood Markets Inc. and Interactive Brokers LLC. 
The company plans to invest the raised capital in strengthening the traditional part of its ecosystem: scaling swap markets, launching a public trading API, and moving swaps toward 24/7 trading. 
The Perpetual Boom Meets a Fractured Regulatory Environment
  Perpetuals are the latest and the hottest trend in the global finance ecosystem. In October, Intercontinental Exchange Inc. invested in Trade [XYZ], which deploys perpetuals for traditional assets on Hyperliquid. 
In November 2026, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in the US allowed perpetual futures on single stocks could begin trading on regulated U.S. exchanges, subject to joint CFTC and SEC oversight. 
In the EU, perpetuals are not explicitly banned for retail traders, but regulators may treat them as derivatives. In the UK, it is strictly forbidden to offer crypto derivatives to retail traders. 
Meanwhile, Variational’s services are not available in the US, Canada and several other prohibited jurisdictions. EU and UK citizens are not excluded, though their access remains subject to local laws and additional platform-level restrictions.


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: Encrypted Account: a PIN that lives in the contract
description:
TL;DR
Encrypted Account is an ERC-4337 smart account that keeps a PIN inside the contract, encrypted under Zama’s threshold FHE. The contract itself checks the PIN and counts the guesses; no server holds either.
Every guess is counted on-chain before its result can be decrypted. The PIN cannot be brute-forced offline, and online guessing is limited to about 12 guesses in 30 days.
The key alone can only pay known addresses within set limits. A new address, a large amount or an arbitrary call needs the PIN and a delay.
A guess that the owner’s second device has not co-signed must carry an ETH bond that doubles with each wrong guess. A wrong guess leaves the bond in the account, so a thief with a stolen key pays the owner for every miss.
The escape needs no FHE. The key alone starts it, and after a delay the funds go to an address the owner chose in advance.
Research prototype on Sepolia, unaudited, MIT.
Motivation
Stolen keys remain the main way self-custody fails. Keys leak through malware, phishing and compromised devices, not only through lost seed phrases. In 2025, Chainalysis counted 158,000 personal-wallet compromises with at least 80,000 victims (The Block).
Today’s defenses move the problem rather than solve it. Co-signer services add a server or a second device to every payment, and social recovery is slow. On-chain spending limits are public, so a thief knows exactly what he can take.
A second factor that the contract checks itself would close this gap. But a knowledge factor on a public chain usually fails in one of two ways. If the data that verifies it is public (a hash, a commitment, a ZK verification key), a 6-digit PIN falls to offline brute force: 10⁶ candidates are too few, even behind a slow hash. If verification happens off-chain (a server, a TEE, an MPC committee), the rate limit lives off-chain too, with its own trust and liveness.
The idea: count first, reveal after
FHE lets the contract hold both the secret and the counter. The PIN fingerprint is stored as a ciphertext, the comparison runs on ciphertexts, and the result is an encrypted bit. The contract decides when that bit may be decrypted, so it can count every attempt before anyone sees its result.
Setup. The client derives h = first64(Argon2id(PIN, salt)) (64 MiB, t = 3; the salt binds the chain and the account) and stores Enc(h). The PIN never leaves the device.
Challenge. Opening an operation emits c = H(tag, chainId, account, opId, opHash), bound to the operation’s content.
Guess. The client sends Enc((h + c) mod 2^64) with an input proof. The account adds a provisional point to the wrong-guess score, compares under FHE and marks only the result bit as decryptable. For a transfer, a second bit gives the delay class; it is masked by the first, so a wrong guess learns nothing about the limits.
Finalize. Anyone relays the threshold network’s signed result. A correct guess removes its own point and starts the operation’s delay; a wrong one keeps the point and starts a back-off.
The contract never reveals the result of a guess it has not counted. A guess is bound to one challenge, so it is useless for any other operation.
client                               account (on-chain)                     threshold network
open(op) ──────────────────────────► emit challenge c
Enc((h + c) mod 2^64) + proof ─────► score += 1, hold the bond
                                     ok = (Enc(h) + c == guess), under FHE
                                     mark only ok decryptable ────────────► decrypt one bit
anyone: finalize(ok, signature) ───► ok: refund the point and the bond, start the delay
                                     wrong: keep both, start a back-off
execute after the delay ───────────► transfer

Design
The key alone covers small payments to known addresses; everything else needs the PIN and a delay, and an escape covers the worst case. A watchtower, an off-chain service the owner names at setup, relays the second phase of each check and alerts the owner. It can only restrict the account and read alarm bits, and it never holds funds.



Two paths. The key (K) alone can pay known recipients up to a daily per-asset limit. Anything else, such as a new recipient, a large amount, an unlimited approval or an arbitrary call, needs K, the PIN and a delay: 1 hour by default, 48 hours for large amounts and arbitrary calls.
Tighten fast, loosen slow. Anything that only tightens the rules, such as removing a known address, lowering a limit, restricting the account or switching off recovery, takes the key alone and applies at once. Loosening takes the PIN and a delay (24 to 72 hours by default).
Hidden rules. In the encrypted-policy variant, the known lists and the limits are ciphertexts, and the real cut-off is a random tripwire below the limit that nobody knows, the owner included. A K-only payment that fails any check moves to the PIN path without saying which. One above the tripwire also sets a sticky alarm that only the watchtower can read, and K-only payments stay blocked until the owner clears it with the PIN.
Rate limit. There is no wait after the first two wrong guesses, then 15 min · 4^(n−3), capped at 7 days; the score decays by one point every 7 days. A correct PIN never resets the score (an early version that did allowed 2,307 guesses in 30 days). A simulation of the contract’s exact rules gives at most 12 guesses in 30 days if the owner does nothing.
Bond. A guess made with the key alone, or by anyone through the recovery track, must carry an ETH bond from outside the account, never from its balance. It starts at 0.001 ETH and doubles with that track’s wrong-guess score: 0.002, 0.004 and so on. A correct guess gets its bond back; a wrong one leaves it in the account, so every miss adds to the owner’s balance. The owner can raise the key-track base up to 100 ETH with a PIN-verified change; the recovery track does not follow it yet (see Limitations).
Second device. Guesses co-signed by the owner’s second device (or a recovery helper) carry no bond and have their own back-off budget, so a thief with the key alone cannot lock the owner out of that path.
Escape. K alone starts it. It cancels every pending operation, closes the anonymous guessing tracks and the K-only path, and fixes the escape address. Signatures. ERC-1271 accepts only hashes approved through a PIN-verified operation, so a permit phished with the key alone is void.

It is on by default, and the key alone can switch it off.
Duress PIN (optional). A second PIN passes the check but sets a silent-alarm bit that only the watchtower can decrypt. The slot is always filled, with FHE randomness when no duress PIN is chosen, so nobody can tell which accounts have one. In open mode it is an alarm, not a brake: the transfer forced out of the owner still goes through.

A thief who steals the seed phrase but not the PIN can take little and pays for every guess.
He can pay addresses already on the known list, up to the hidden daily limit. A payment that fails a check moves to the PIN path without saying which, and one above the tripwire sets off a silent alarm.
He cannot pay his own address or move a large amount without the PIN, and a permit signed with the key alone is void.
He can guess the PIN about 12 times in 30 days, paying a doubling bond each time: about 0.65 ETH in total at the default base. Every wrong guess pays the owner and triggers an alert, and three wrong guesses on the key track restrict the account, which stops key-only payments.
The owner answers with the escape. Once it starts, guessing and key-only payments stop, and after the delay the funds land at the escape address.
With human-chosen 6-digit PINs and no blocklist, 12 throttled guesses succeed about 7% of the time, and 4 guesses (an escape within the first hour) about 2.6% (Markert et al., IEEE S&P 2020). Below 10 guesses the curve is interpolated linearly, so the second figure is optimistic. With a random PIN from the app’s generator, 12 guesses succeed about 0.0015% of the time. The app offers a random PIN, rejects only a short list of the most common PINs and warns about other guessable ones.
A thief who does find the PIN still waits out the PIN-path delay, and the owner’s escape cancels the pending operation.
What you have to trust
Every second factor moves trust somewhere; the question is where.
Second factor
Checked by

Co-signer service (SMS, email or app code)
A company’s server
Its honesty and uptime; it sees every payment


TEE enclave
A secure chip run by an operator
The chip vendor, side channels and the operator’s uptime

A group of share holders
That enough of them never collude, and their uptime


Passkey or fingerprint
The phone’s secure chip
The phone and its vendor; whoever unlocks the phone can sign


Email recovery
The email provider
The provider’s signing keys and the inbox


Multisig (k of n)
The chain
That k keys are never taken together; the rules are public


Encrypted Account
The contract, under FHE
Zama’s threshold network and its governance




In the first five rows, a party off-chain decides whether the second factor is right. A multisig decides on-chain but needs several keys for every payment and shows its rules to a thief. The FHE PIN decides on-chain too, with the counter and the rules hidden, so no server holds the PIN or decides on the limit. The trust that remains sits in a threshold network rather than one operator, and the escape does not depend even on that.
With a multisig or a passkey. The designs compose:
An Encrypted Account can be one signer of a multisig. Its ERC-1271 signature exists only for hashes approved with the PIN and a delay, so a stolen key of that signer cannot co-sign.
A multisig can be the account’s key: it calls the account directly, so key-only payments need its quorum and everything else still needs the PIN.
The escape address can be a cold multisig, which consents to its role with an ERC-1271 signature.
The second device can be a passkey behind an ERC-1271 wrapper, so a fingerprint co-signs the guesses that need no bond.
We have not tested these combinations yet.
Status and cost
Encrypted Account is a research prototype: unaudited, testnet only, MIT. Measured on Sepolia with the public testnet relayer and KMS:
What
Result




PIN flow, end to end (desktop client, N = 30)
p50 24.4 s, p95 47.7 s


Input proof on a mid-range phone
p95 13.65 s


PIN-verified transfer (request, guess, finalize, execute)
≈ 2.7M gas


Key-only transfer, encrypted lists and limit
≈ 1.76M gas


Key-only transfer, public lists and limit
≈ 60k gas




Sepolia already prices a new storage slot about five times higher than mainnet does today, and FHE state is storage-heavy. On today’s mainnet schedule, the first two transfers model to about 1.8M and 1.1M gas. The public-list variant gives up the hidden lists, limit and tripwire for a key-only transfer about 30 times cheaper.
The repository also contains a hidden will (heirs with encrypted shares), which this post leaves out.
Limitations and open questions
Like any FHE application, the design inherits the trust assumptions of Zama’s network, and a few edges are still open.
Trust in Zama. Confidentiality relies on Zama’s threshold KMS, which fails if 5 of its 13 nodes collude. Integrity relies on an honest majority of coprocessors, and both rely on contracts that Zama’s governance can upgrade.
A leaked fingerprint. If the network leaks h, the PIN check is bypassed, and about 10⁶ Argon2id runs recover the PIN itself: roughly two days on one core, about an hour on a large server. With seedless recovery on, that leak plus 7 days without a reaction from the owner (30 with a registered second device) is enough to take over an account. Ciphertexts stay on-chain, so a key that leaks later opens today’s fingerprints too.
A side door for the bond. The recovery track still prices guesses from 0.001 ETH, whatever base the owner set for the key track, and the two tracks share one budget. Until both follow the owner’s base, a raised base can be sidestepped there.
Griefing. Through the same shared budget, a stranger can push the owner’s PIN back-off to 7 days for about 0.26 ETH in bonds, which stay in the account. Owners with a second device keep their own path, and key-only payments and the escape still work.
Visibility and devices. In open mode, balances, amounts and recipients are public; only the rules are encrypted. A private mode with ERC-7984 tokens is in progress. If the key and the PIN are entered in the same browser, a compromised front end gets both.
Open questions
In FHEVM, every persistent permission on a ciphertext is a new storage slot. As state creation gets more expensive, which patterns should apps use: transient or persistent permissions, and reusable records instead of per-operation ones?
Should seedless recovery be on by default, and with what delay and bond?
Is a standard worth it, for example an ERC-7579 module with a PIN-gated operation lifecycle and escape semantics?
Feedback is welcome, especially on the threat model, the rate-limit rules and the bond.
Links
Code (MIT), measurement method and raw data: github.com/Himess/encrypted-account (RESULTS.md, results/)
Live demo on Sepolia: encrypted-account.vercel.app

title: Fed Minutes Signal More Hikes – Why Bitcoin Should Care
description:
Summary Markets did part of the Fed’s tightening. The bigger risk is a steeper path. Yields and risk appetite hit […]
The post Fed Minutes Signal More Hikes – Why Bitcoin Should Care appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Summary

  • Markets did part of the Fed’s tightening.
  • The bigger risk is a steeper path.
  • Yields and risk appetite hit Bitcoin differently.
  • November CPI arrives a day after the vote.

The Federal Reserve published the minutes of its October 27-28 meeting at 19:00 UTC on November 18, three weeks before its next decision.

Markets did part of the Fed’s work

Officials held the target range at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 vote. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase, a hawkish split behind the October pause.

The full meeting record shows how firmly hikes stayed on the table. Almost all participants judged that further action to raise the target range would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks, with the aim of returning inflation to 2% in a timely way.

That consensus is also why the majority could wait. Some participants said market-implied tightening for December and next year was broadly consistent with their own view of the right path, and several took that alignment as a reason why holding steady carried less risk.

When markets price hikes in advance, borrowing costs often rise before the Fed votes. A pause in October therefore did not mean easier conditions for crypto; futures and yields were already doing part of the tightening.

A couple of participants went further, saying an increase larger than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if incoming inflation data proved unfavorable. That was a conditional view from a small group, recorded in October, not a committee plan.

Futures pricing shows how little of that December step is left to surprise. As of the evening of November 18, the CME FedWatch tool, which derives probabilities from fed funds futures, put the chance of a December hike at 100%: 90.7% for a quarter point to 4.00%-4.25% and 9.3% for a half point to 4.25%-4.50%. That 9.3% is the market’s price on the larger move a couple of officials discussed, and the figure to watch as new data arrives before the vote.

The path behind the next hike

The minutes also report the median expectation from the New York Fed trading desk’s survey of market participants: one hike in December, another in March 2027, and a cut in early 2028. Collected before the meeting, it is the clearest snapshot in the document of where investors thought rates were heading.

Under that survey path, the range would reach 4.25%-4.50% after March and stay there until early 2028. With futures treating a December hike as settled, a quarter-point move adds little new information for Bitcoin. Pressure would come from a revision to the path itself, and there are three ways it could get steeper.

Step one, bigger

A December move above 25 basis points would front-load tightening and test positions built around a quarter point.

A third hike

Another increase after March would lift the expected peak, the level that sets how much idle dollars can earn.

A later first cut

Pushing relief beyond early 2028 would extend the stretch in which interest-bearing assets compete with a coin that pays nothing.

Two routes from the rate path to Bitcoin

The first route is yield competition. Bitcoin pays no interest, so every month that Treasury bills and money-market funds pay close to the policy rate raises the return a holder gives up. This route depends mostly on the level of rates and how long it lasts, which is why the timing of the first cut weighs as heavily as December’s decision.

Leveraged traders feel a version of this through borrowing costs, though not one-for-one. Exchange margin rates follow each platform’s terms, DeFi lending rates move with pool demand, and perpetual-futures funding depends on the balance between longs and shorts rather than on the Fed’s benchmark.

The second route is risk appetite. A 2023 IMF working paper by Natasha Che, Alexander Copestake, Davide Furceri and Tammaro Terracciano found that a single common factor explains about 80% of crypto price variation, and that US tightening weakened it through investors’ willingness to take risk, the same channel that moves stocks. The authors read the result as evidence against crypto working as a hedge.

The two routes react to different news. Yield competition builds slowly with the level and duration of rates, while risk appetite responds to surprises that change how much uncertainty investors are prepared to carry. A steeper path would work through both at once. The IMF study supports the direction of that effect but gives no size for any single decision.

READ MORE:

Grayscale Reveals ‘Compelling Entry Points’ but Data Says No

The data calendar into December 9

The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes October’s personal income and outlays report, which carries the PCE price index the Fed targets, at 13:30 UTC on November 25, according to its release schedule. The Bureau of Labor Statistics follows with November’s employment report on December 4.

November’s consumer price index is due on December 10, the day after the decision, per the BLS calendar. That makes October PCE the last major inflation report before the vote, and the most direct test of the “unfavorable data” condition behind the larger-hike view.

Bitcoin’s own flows, from ETF demand to derivatives positioning, will move the price alongside those numbers, so no single print explains a move by itself. The rate question for crypto over the next three weeks is narrower: whether the data bends the path the survey described, through a bigger December step, a hike after March or a later first cut. A quarter-point hike in line with that survey would leave the picture where the October minutes found it.

The post Fed Minutes Signal More Hikes – Why Bitcoin Should Care appeared first on Coindoo.

description:

Eligible non-U.S. users in permitted jurisdictions can earn variable vault income. They keep exposure to the underlying S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 ETF trackers. Subscriptions run through Bitget Earn. Users do not open a separate DeFi wallet or […]
The post Bitget Opens Tokenized ETF Onchain Yield Without a DeFi Wallet appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
Bitget launched rToken Earn on November 16, 2026, opening tokenized ETF onchain yield for Reality-issued rSPY and rQQQ. Eligible non-U.S. users in permitted jurisdictions can earn variable vault income. They keep exposure to the underlying S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 ETF trackers. Subscriptions run through Bitget Earn. Users do not open a separate DeFi wallet or talk to vault contracts themselves.

The Bitget release frames the product as the next use of rTokens after trading and collateral. Bitget handles subscriptions and redemptions on the user's behalf, with no fixed term. Yields are variable and not guaranteed. Availability still depends on jurisdiction and eligibility.

How Tokenized ETF Onchain Yield Moves on Subscribe

The puzzle is not that index ETFs can sit as tokens. Brokers and crypto venues have sold equity-like exposure through wrappers for years. The claim here is narrower. A 1:1-backed tokenized ETF claim can leave the trade screen and enter programmable lending rails. The holder does not have to become a DeFi operator.

Reality issues the rTokens and says each unit is backed 1:1 by the corresponding securities held through its custody path. Ember Protocol supplies the vault infrastructure. Fluid supplies the lending markets and liquidity the strategy uses. Bitget sits in front as the account layer that takes the order, routes the deposit, and brings back the redemption.

Follow one subscription through the stack. An eligible user holds rSPY or rQQQ in a Bitget account. That user joins the matching Earn vault. Bitget moves the tokens into the Ember vault path. The strategy places that collateral into Fluid lending markets. Any yield that returns is variable product income, not a fixed coupon. It is also not a promise that the index return itself is enhanced.

That is tokenized ETF onchain yield as plumbing. Index exposure stays the claim. Income is a separate lending overlay on the same tokens.

Why the Rails Matter, and Where the Catch Sits

Tokenized equities only change capital markets if the claim can do more than trade. Trade and collateral already proved demand for rTokens. Bitget cites DeFiLlama Research figures of more than $1.86 billion in cumulative rToken trading volume between June and July 2026. In October it added rToken Stock Transfer, a two-step path for eligible users to convert supported brokerage holdings into rTokens. Earn is the income layer on top of that catalogue.

Bitwise Investment Manager, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of Bitwise Asset Management, is set to curate the vault strategy. That curation service is not live at launch. Bitget says it will roll out later. Until then, the live surfaces are Ember vaults, Fluid lending, Reality issuance, and Bitget's Earn front end.

"An asset should not be limited to just one purpose," Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said in the release. Jonathan Man, portfolio manager at Bitwise, called tokenization the first step and putting the assets to work the next one. Ember co-founder Ibra Barbery framed the point as infrastructure users should not have to think about. Fluid founder and CEO Samyak Jain cast lending as the engine that now reaches widely held traditional assets onchain.

The catch is the usual one for AI and blockchain readers watching tokenization infra. A packaged Earn product hides wallet friction. It does not hide smart-contract, oracle, liquidity, or counterparty risk on the vault and lending path. U.S. persons stay outside. Yield is not guaranteed. Bitwise curation is still ahead of the switch. The release also skips a live APY and a TVL figure for the new vaults. It gives no independent proof of how deep Fluid liquidity is for these tokens on day one.

What Is Proven, and What Is Not

What the primary record shows is concrete. Bitget opened rToken Earn for rSPY and rQQQ on November 16, 2026. Reality issues the tokens with a 1:1 securities-backing claim. Ember and Fluid are named as vault and lending rails. Access runs through Bitget Earn for eligible non-U.S. users. Bitwise strategy curation is disclosed as a later rollout.

What remains open is harder. The launch does not prove durable income versus holding the cash-market ETFs. It also does not prove every eligible jurisdiction will keep the product available as rules shift. It does not prove that tokenized index claims behave like registered fund shares in every local legal sense once they sit in a lending vault.

The sharper model is simple. Tokenized ETF onchain yield here is not a new index fund. It is custody-backed index tokens plugged into programmable collateral rails behind an exchange account. Watch whether Bitwise curation arrives. Watch whether vault balances grow past launch marketing. Watch whether the same Earn path widens beyond rSPY and rQQQ without forcing users back into a separate DeFi wallet.

The post Bitget Opens Tokenized ETF Onchain Yield Without a DeFi Wallet appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.

title: XRP Price Was Worth Less Than a Penny When GTA 5 Launched: Could GTA 6 See It Hit $100?
description:
XRP was trading below a cent when GTA5 arrived. Thirteen years later, GTA6 is going to be released while XRP has became a financial giant.
The post XRP Price Was Worth Less Than a Penny When GTA 5 Launched: Could GTA 6 See It Hit $100? appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
XRP price was trading below one cent when Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013. Thirteen years later, Rockstar is preparing to release GTA 6, while XRP has grown into one of the largest cryptos. XRP is a financial giant today.

The comparison is striking. On September 17, 2013, the day GTA V launched, XRP was trading at $0.009613. Today, XRP trades near $0.95, representing a price gain of almost 100 times from that launch-day price.

But can XRP deliver another extraordinary rally as GTA 6 arrives? A $100 price target would turn a relatively small crypto investment into a fortune, but it would also require XRP to reach a market valuation never seen before in the crypto industry.

Xrp (XRP)
24h7d30d1yAll time

Discover: The Best Token Presales

From GTA 5 Penny-Stock Era to XRP Multi-Dollar Price Rally

When GTA V introduced players to Los Santos in 2013, XRP was still largely flying under the radar. Its price sat below one cent, and its market cap was ranging around $75 million. Then the following years changed everything.

XRP broke above $0.10 in May 2017 before accelerating during the historic crypto bull market. By December 2017, the token had crossed $1 and continued climbing toward its January 2018 all-time high of $3.84.

That is an extraordinary transformation from its GTA V launch-day price. A $1,000 investment at $0.009613 would have purchased more than 100,000 XRP. At $3.84, that position would have been worth nearly $400,000. Something that only crypto can do.

However, XRP’s journey was far from smooth. The token endured successive bear markets, regulatory uncertainty, and the SEC’s lawsuit against Ripple in December 2020. Its recovery eventually pushed XRP back toward record territory in 2025, when it reached $3.65.

Now, XRP is trading around $0.95, substantially below its previous peaks. Will another major recovery begin before GTA 6 is released?

GTA 6 Could Be the Start of XRP’s Next $100 Chapter

Rockstar’s GTA 6 arrives more than 13 years after GTA V, creating an interesting milestone for XRP investors. XRP has experienced multiple market cycles during the same period, transforming from a sub-penny asset into a major digital currency.

XRP currently has 63.5 billion tokens in circulation. At $100 per token, its market capitalization would reach $6.35 trillion. That would put XRP among the most valuable financial assets in the world, exceeding the market capitalization of most publicly traded companies.

The bullish argument rests on XRP’s potential to capture a much larger share of institutional payments, cross-border settlements, and digital asset liquidity. Ripple has spent years building financial infrastructure around the XRP Ledger, while institutional interest in crypto investment products continues to develop.

A stronger crypto market could also provide the liquidity needed for another substantial XRP rally. But XRP would need considerably more capital, adoption, and sustained demand to justify a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

The historical comparison remains fascinating. XRP went from less than a penny when GTA V launched to several dollars during subsequent crypto cycles. Few people back then would have believed XRP could get to where it is now.

description:

The post Florida Man Sentenced in North Carolina to 51 Months for $800,000 Cell Phone Tower Fraud Scheme appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
Federal prosecutors have secured a 51-month prison sentence against a Florida man who ran a fraudulent cell phone tower consulting scheme that collected more than $800,000 from hundreds of victims.

Alexander Francise Blasscyk, 48, of Windermere, Florida, was sentenced in federal court in Charlotte, North Carolina, to 51 months in prison plus three years of supervised release and ordered to pay $1,039,115.30 in restitution, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of North Carolina.

According to court documents, Blasscyk defrauded victims by falsely claiming to be a cell tower consultant. Between 2018 and 2024, he told individuals, including residents of Ashe County, that he would market their properties to cell tower companies and wireless carriers for a fee. He also promised to negotiate lease agreements that would allow the companies to build towers on their land in exchange for rental payments.

Hundreds of victims, including individuals and businesses, paid Blasscyk or companies he controlled more than $800,000 for the purported consulting services and related expenses. However, little to no work was performed. Blasscyk did not market the properties to wireless carriers or cell tower companies as promised, nor did he negotiate the lease agreements he had offered to secure.

To persuade victims to hand over their money, Blasscyk provided false and fraudulent documents through his company.

Blasscyk used two companies to solicit fees for nonexistent work marketing land for tower leases and instead spent the money on personal expenses, including hotels, short-term rentals, restaurants and bars.

U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson said the defendant gave people the hope of passive income.

“Blasscyk gave people the hope of passive income — making false promises to lease land to cell phone tower companies while collecting consulting fees. But Blasscyk did no consulting, made no such deals, and created fake documents to cover up his fraud.”

He pleaded guilty to wire fraud in October 2025.
