title: Nuvera Opens All-Hours Polygon Stablecoin Settlement
description:
Polygon Labs said on November 18, 2026, that Nuvera Polygon stablecoin settlement is live on Open Money Stack. Customers can still fund dollar accounts by bank transfer. Then they can move the money onward as a stablecoin at any hour through the OMS dashboard. That path sits beside waiting on correspondent banking cutoffs. The Polygon […]
The post Nuvera Opens All-Hours Polygon Stablecoin Settlement appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
Polygon Labs said on November 18, 2026, that Nuvera Polygon stablecoin settlement is live on Open Money Stack. Customers can still fund dollar accounts by bank transfer. Then they can move the money onward as a stablecoin at any hour through the OMS dashboard. That path sits beside waiting on correspondent banking cutoffs. The Polygon Labs post is the primary record for the go-live.

That is the news. A cross-border payments firm kept the bank-transfer front door. It put the onchain hop behind it.

How Nuvera Polygon Stablecoin Settlement Works

Nuvera builds payments rails for importers, exporters, and firms that pay suppliers across regions. Its customers sit in the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Africa. The company says it uses local rails where they exist. It uses SWIFT where they do not. It uses stablecoins when faster settlement is the job. Its tagline frames the harder markets plainly: "Unbanked isn't unbankable."

With Polygon OMS, the customer path stays familiar at the start. A business pays in by bank transfer. The transfer lands in a dollar account Nuvera issues. Nuvera's team can then move the funds onward as a stablecoin. That hop runs through the OMS dashboard around the clock.

Marcelo Correa, Nuvera's Chief Business Officer, put the product test in one line in the Polygon post. Customers judge the firm on how quickly and predictably money arrives. Polygon OMS lets Nuvera settle in stablecoins. It keeps the bank-transfer experience those customers already expect.

What Polygon Open Money Stack Adds

Polygon Open Money Stack is Polygon's stack for moving money across bank accounts, cards, cash, and wallets. The pitch is one integration surface for payments companies. It is not a duct-taped rail for each step. That design sits in the same lane as earlier bank-to-stablecoin transfer experiments on Polygon rails.

On the outbound side, Polygon says OMS can send to bank accounts and cash pickup points. It can also send to wallets on Polygon, Ethereum, and Solana. Cash and debit cards sit on the pay-in side of the same stack. Agent payments with preset limits are part of the broader OMS story. They are not the Nuvera customer flow announced today.

The practical stake for Nuvera's users is timing. An overseas invoice may need to clear after a bank's cutoff. The onward leg can still settle in a stablecoin. The bank transfer still has to land. What changes after that landing is the settlement clock.

What a Bank-to-Stablecoin Settlement Path Is Actually Telling You

Here is the recurring question this go-live presses. When a private dollar token says it is worth one dollar, what does wiring it behind a bank pay-in prove?

It does not invent a new peg. It does not replace Nuvera's bank relationships. It proves a settlement handoff. Customers keep funding the way they already fund. The money can keep moving after banking hours. The next hop is onchain.

That is a different story from listing a stablecoin on an exchange. It is also different from parking float in DeFi. Cross-border payments firms get hired for speed and predictability. Correspondent banking cutoffs are the failure mode those customers already know. Today's launch is a bet on the bank-transfer front door. The back office can stop treating evening as a hard stop.

Unknowns remain. The Polygon post does not publish live settlement volumes or fee schedules. It also skips a full country list for Nuvera dollar accounts. It does not name which stablecoin tickers sit on every outbound route. Licensing claims and bank relationships stay high level. Production proof will show up in arrival times, not in the launch post.

The peg promise is still the same question it always was. Can a familiar bank pay-in feed an all-hours stablecoin settlement leg? And can it do that without asking the customer to become a crypto operator first?

title: Bitcoin's 3rd Phase COMPLETE
Why Bitcoin’s Order Book Can Fool You
description:
The short version Depth shows quantity, not how fast it changes. Book Churn counts price-level updates every ten minutes. Volatility […]
The post Why Bitcoin’s Order Book Can Fool You appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
The short version

  • Depth shows quantity, not how fast it changes.
  • Book Churn counts price-level updates every ten minutes.
  • Volatility hit rate: 63% against a 50% baseline.
  • A simple price-range signal matched it.

Glassnode’s November 18 research built the metric from Binance perpetual futures data, with Bitcoin and Ether backfilled to January 2020. The results hold up against random noise. They barely beat a far simpler measure.

What Book Churn actually counts

Binance streams every change to its order book as it happens. Each message says, in effect, that a given price now holds a new quantity of bids or asks. Trades trigger messages too, because a fill shrinks what rests at that price. Glassnode adds these messages up in ten-minute windows. On BTCUSDT, a typical window carries about 607,000.

A raw count needs context. Glassnode turns it into a score by measuring each window against the same clock hour over the previous 30 days, so a busy trading hour faces its own history and the dead of night faces its own. A score of 2 marks an unusually active window. Readings of 3 or more are rarer still.

The feed has blind spots. It reports price levels, not individual orders, so one message can bundle several cancels, new orders and fills. It doesn’t separate a pulled quote from an executed one, and it names no traders. When the exchange connection drops and resets, a window can even read quieter than it was. A spike tells you the book got busy. It can’t tell you why.

Two books, one screenshot

Picture two order books with identical quantities at every price. Same depth. Same spread. A screenshot can’t tell them apart, but ten minutes of watching can: in Glassnode’s illustration, one book changes 14 times and the other 56. Those counts are invented to show the idea. The point behind them is real. Depth tells you how much is resting, churn tells you how often it moves, and neither metric answers the other’s question.

April 27: the book barely flinched, the feed tripled

Depth here means the dollar value of bids and asks resting within 1% of the mid-price. The spread is the gap between the best bid and the best ask. On the morning of April 27, both looked calm.

Three windows starting at 05:10, 05:20 and 05:30 UTC carried 1.8 million to 2.1 million updates each, up from 0.6 million to 0.9 million in the hour before. Churn scores hit 4.34, 3.83 and 3.41. Combined depth, which had ranged between $400 million and $464 million in the prior hour, slipped to between $377 million and $412 million. Then it jumped to $565 million in the next window. The spread sat at about one tick throughout.

Price didn’t sit still. The high-to-low range reached 95 basis points, close to 1%, in the first burst window, then 28 and 39 basis points in the next two. Range shows how far price traveled inside a window, not which way it finished.

So a trader watching depth and spread saw a mild dip. Underneath, the update feed nearly tripled.

Most busy windows don’t look like this. Across BTCUSDT history, higher churn usually came with thinner depth and wider spreads, with correlations of -0.40 and +0.49 respectively. The case that matters most, with normal depth, quiet prices and frantic quoting all at once, showed up in only about 7% of BTCUSDT readings at 3 or above. Those are the windows where churn picks up something nothing else on the screen shows.

Keep the scope in mind. This is one perpetual futures contract on one exchange, not the whole Bitcoin market. And combined depth counts both sides of the book, so a buyer can only draw on the asks, a fraction of that total.

Where churn meets your fill

A market buy takes the cheapest ask first, then the next one up, and keeps climbing until the order is complete. Coinbase’s trading rules spell out that a single market order can fill at several prices. Here’s a made-up book, shown twice: once as you saw it, and once after a single quote moved.

Hypothetical asks, buying 3 BTC
Ask price Book A: as seen Book B: one quote moved
$100,000 1 BTC none
$100,100 1 BTC 1 BTC
$100,150 none 1 BTC
$100,200 3 BTC 3 BTC
Cost of 3 BTC $300,300 $300,450

In Book A, a 3 BTC market buy pays $100,000, $100,100 and $100,200, an average of $100,100 before fees. Anyone expecting the whole order at the top price pays $300 more than planned. Thin depth at the best ask did that. Churn played no part.

Book B is where churn comes in. The seller at $100,000 pulls that coin and reposts it at $100,150 a moment before your order lands. You see the same screen and send the same order, and you pay $450 above the top-of-book estimate. Repeat that kind of swap across thousands of price levels and you get a churn spike. The score can’t say which level will move, or where it goes next.

A limit order caps the price but may leave you partly filled, or not filled at all. Coindoo’s guide to how crypto orders execute covers that trade-off, and fees sit on top of every figure above, as our breakdown of Bitcoin buying costs shows.

63% sounds strong. The baseline is 50%.

Glassnode’s main test asked a narrow question. When churn scored 2 or higher, was the next hour more volatile than the median hour? Half of all hours land above the median by definition, so a coin flip scores 50%.

Share of signals followed by an above-median volatility hour. Source: Glassnode
Signal BTCUSDT ETHUSDT
Random placebo spikes 51.2% 50.5%
Churn reading from 24 hours earlier 58.9% 58.4%
Churn score 2 or higher 63.2% 63.4%
Price-range signal 63.7% 63.5%
Churn score 3 or higher 69.1% 68.2%

Start at the top. Random spikes land right on the coin flip, which tells you the test isn’t rigged. Churn clears that line, and higher scores clear it by more.

The highlighted row is the awkward one. Glassnode built a matching signal from nothing but each window’s high-to-low swing, and it edged churn by a fraction of a point, a gap too small to call either way. The two scores move together with a correlation of 0.84. Price range alone explains about 70% of the variation in the churn score. For the most part, churn re-measures price movement through the quote feed.

Not entirely, though. In roughly half the windows where churn fired, the range signal stayed silent. Similar accuracy, different moments.

The day-old row tells its own story. A reading from a full day earlier kept most of the edge, which points to volatility that lingers for days, while the current reading adds four to five points on top. And about 37% of high readings still came before a perfectly ordinary hour.

Glassnode lists its own limits. The test ran in-sample: volatility buckets and control groups were set using each full calendar year, including months a live trader wouldn’t have seen yet. Results for 2020 and 2021 came in at 53% to 57%, not clearly above chance. By Glassnode’s own description, Bitcoin and Ether on one exchange amount to close to a single test. The score says nothing about direction, and the study never measured trading returns or execution costs.

READ MORE:

XRP Ledger’s Big Bank Test Covered Only 2 of 10 Rules

Before you send a large order

Check the ask side at your own order size. A combined depth figure blends buyers and sellers, and the best price usually covers only the first slice of a big order.

During a churn spike, read a one-tick spread as a fact about the best price and nothing deeper. The next level up may be the one getting rewritten.

Then decide which risk you would rather carry. A market order gets the trade done at an unknown price. A limit order holds the price and may never fill.

Glassnode hasn’t tested whether churn improves real fills once depth, spread and fees enter the math. It also doesn’t publish how long each reading takes to arrive after its window closes, which matters to anyone hoping to act on one. What the metric does today is narrower and still worth having. When updates triple and the spread doesn’t budge, the calm you see is only the top layer.

Why AI-ROC Is the Future of Exposure Management
description: Executive Summary Security teams have never had better visibility into their assets, vulnerabilities, and threats. What they lack is the speed to act on it. Frontier AI models are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than ever, attackers are using the same models to exploit them within hours, and most remediation still depends on scans, tickets, and change […]
fullContent:
Executive Summary

Security teams have never had better visibility into their assets, vulnerabilities, and threats. What they lack is the speed to act on it. Frontier AI models are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than ever, attackers are using the same models to exploit them within hours, and most remediation still depends on scans, tickets, and change windows. Exposure management needs a new operating model that detects exposures as soon as they are disclosed, focuses only on what is proven exploitable, and remediates autonomously without breaking the business. That operating model is the AI-native Risk Operations Center (AI-ROC).

On October 13, 2026, Microsoft released the largest Patch Tuesday in its history, fixing 1,414 vulnerabilities. That is more than seven times the 193 vulnerabilities Microsoft fixed in October 2025. One of the new vulnerabilities was already being exploited, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) set a deadline of just three days to patch it.

At ROCon Americas 2026, we made the case that most organizations are focused on the wrong question. Knowing how many exposures you have is no longer useful on its own. What matters is how quickly you can turn those exposures into verified risk reduction.

The Vulnerability Surge Has Outpaced Remediation

Over the last twenty years, the security industry has gotten very good at finding things. Organizations now have more data on assets, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, threat intelligence, and alerts than ever before. The ability to fix what matters has not kept up.

Frontier AI has made that gap much wider. These models are not creating new vulnerabilities. They are surfacing flaws that already existed in code, and they are doing it much faster than before. The last two Patch Tuesdays, with 974 vulnerabilities in September and more than 1,400 in October, show how fast this is moving. Attackers have access to the same AI tools and are using them to weaponize new vulnerabilities within hours. In September, two of the vulnerabilities Microsoft disclosed were already being exploited before a patch was available.

The way most organizations remediate has barely changed. A scanner detects the vulnerability, a second tool adds asset context, a third ranks it, an attack simulation tool tests it, and a ticket is created in the hope that someone fixes it within a 30- or 60-day service-level agreement (SLA). Each of those handoffs adds time, and risk only goes down when the fix is actually applied. This process was not built for attackers who move in hours.

What the Surge Means for Security Teams

Remediation timelines are shrinking from weeks to days, but the resources to meet them are not keeping pace.

  • SLAs are moving from weeks to days. The 30- and 60-day SLAs most programs were built around no longer match the threat. Critical vulnerabilities now need to be patched in days, and mandates from CISA and CERT-In, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, can require remediation in as little as 12 to 24 hours.
  • Exploitation is how most breaches now start. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days.
  • Budgets and headcount are not keeping pace. Only 15% of security leaders expect their budgets to grow by more than 10%. Hiring more analysts is not a realistic answer.
  • There are too many findings to fix. One large Qualys customer had 62.5 million findings. No team has the time or budget to work through that many.

The Ideal Operating Model for Exposure Management

None of this is a new problem. Exposure management still comes down to the same basics of visibility, prioritization, and remediation. What has changed is the speed at which each of them has to happen.

  • Detection must happen in real time. New exposures should be identified as soon as a vulnerability is disclosed, not after the next scheduled scan.
  • Prioritization must be based on proof. Risk scores tell you what could be dangerous. Teams need to know whether an attacker can actually reach and exploit the vulnerability in their environment.
  • Remediation must take hours, not a month. Low-risk fixes should be automated, and every fix should be checked to confirm it worked.

These steps also need to run on one platform. Every handoff between separate tools and teams adds delay, and that delay is the window attackers use.

Qualys calls this operating model the Risk Operations Center (ROC). When AI agents handle the time-sensitive work at each stage, it becomes an AI-native ROC, or AI-ROC.

How Qualys Operationalizes the AI-ROC

The Qualys AI-ROC brings this operating model together on the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management Platform. It pulls in every asset and exposure across cloud, on-premises, operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT), mobile, and AI environments, enriches them with threat intelligence and business context, and then prioritizes and remediates the risk that matters. Three AI agents handle the work that has to happen at machine speed: Agent Insta for detection, Agent Val for validation, and Agent Sara for remediation.

AI-Speed Detection with InstaScan

With traditional scanning, a vendor has to write a detection signature, roll it out, and then customers have to rescan their environment. That can take a day or two before a team even knows it is affected. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, monitors vendor advisories around the clock and matches them against the asset and software data customers already have. No new scan is needed. After the October release, Agent Insta customers had detections within five minutes.

Hyper-Prioritization with TruConfirm

Even after applying threat intelligence and business context, a large organization can still be left with hundreds of thousands of findings. TruConfirm, powered by Agent Val, tests whether those findings can actually be exploited in the customer’s environment, using production-safe payloads that never download malware. For the customer mentioned above, this reduced 62.5 million findings to 60,000 that were confirmed exploitable.

Zero-Day Remediation with TruRisk Eliminate

Detection and prioritization only matter if the risk gets fixed. Before launching TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, we kept asking why teams were not remediating faster. Automation was not the blocker, since patch automation tools have existed for years. Confidence was. Teams did not know whether they were choosing the right fix, whether a patch would crash a business application, or whether compensating controls already covered the risk.

TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence is built to answer those questions and to be the system of record and system of action for cyber risk reduction. It takes prioritized findings from Qualys or third-party tools and recommends the right fix for each one. A patch reliability score shows how likely a patch is to deploy without issues, and integrations with firewalls and other controls show when a compensating control already covers the risk. Patching is not always the answer. If a company has moved from Zoom to Microsoft Teams and a Zoom zero-day is disclosed, the right action is to uninstall Zoom rather than patch it.

Agent Sara plans the rollout. Low-impact updates such as browsers and standalone utilities are patched automatically with no reboot required. Production workloads are patched in rings, starting in a lab environment, with health monitoring through partners like Dynatrace. If CPU, memory, or network indicators show a problem, Agent Sara stops the rollout and rolls the patch back. When a patch is not safe to deploy, Agent Sara applies a mitigation instead.

Trust Is Built Into the AI-ROC

As soon as agents start remediating, security and IT teams ask the same four questions. The AI-ROC answers each one with a setting the team controls.

  • What breaks if the agent gets it wrong? Every patch carries an AI reliability score based on real-world deployments. Dependency and downtime impact are known before anything is approved, and rollback is staged in advance.
  • Can we start small and prove it? Deployment waves let teams start with zero-touch automation for low-impact fixes, use ring-based rollouts for everything else, and keep tighter control over their most critical systems. Each team decides where to start.
  • How do I know why it did that? ROCky, the Qualys conversational AI interface, and every agent show their reasoning, including the threat, the affected asset, any compensating control, and the TruConfirm evidence behind each action.
  • Can I take the wheel back? Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback happens automatically if a service degrades, and nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

Policy, risk appetite, confidence thresholds, approval gates, and exceptions stay with the security team, and the agents work within those boundaries. Autonomy is not something teams have to take on faith. They control how much of it to use, and the program can grow with the environment instead of with headcount.

How the Three Agents Handle a Zero-Day

At ROCon, we walked through how the agents worked together on CVE-2026-81963, a Windows vulnerability from the September Patch Tuesday that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on the same day. Agent Insta detected it in the customer’s environment within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val confirmed it was exploitable on the customer’s assets. Agent Sara saw that the patch required a reboot and already had a low reliability score, so it deployed to the lab environment first. When health indicators showed issues, Agent Sara rolled the patch back and applied a temporary mitigation, reducing the risk without the patch ever reaching production.

What Comes Next for the AI-ROC

Organizations can adopt the AI-ROC in stages. The journey begins with AI-speed detection, then extends CTEM across every tool already in use, moves to autonomous risk elimination, and finally quantifies cyber risk in business terms for the chief information security officer (CISO), the chief financial officer (CFO), and the board. Each stage builds on the one before it, so teams see results early while working toward a fully autonomous program.

The AI-ROC will continue to grow with the attack surface. As applications, AI systems, and more advanced attack techniques create new kinds of exposure, they will come into the same platform, the same risk view, and the same agent-driven workflows.

Agentic ROC Studio and the Future of Agentic AI in Risk Operations

The next step is Agentic ROC Studio, a concept Qualys is building toward. Every security team has its own runbooks, its own tools, and its own way of working, and no set of prebuilt agents can cover all of it. Agentic ROC Studio is designed to let teams build agents around how they already operate. A team would describe what an agent should do in plain language, choose the tools it is allowed to use, and have it running in minutes, with no scripting required.

These agents would work alongside the Qualys AI agents for exposure, threat, patch, and compliance, and connect to third-party tools and agents across security, IT, cloud, and identity to run as one cross-domain workflow. That is where agentic AI in risk operations is headed: a digital workforce that takes on the repetitive work across the entire risk program, while the security team sets the rules and stays in the loop.

Conclusion

Frontier AI has changed the pace of vulnerability management. Record Patch Tuesdays have arrived for two consecutive months; attackers can weaponize new flaws within hours, and the SLAs most programs were built on no longer hold. Adding more scanners, more findings, and more tickets will not close that gap.

What closes it is an operating model built for AI speed. That means detecting new vulnerabilities as soon as they are disclosed, proving which ones can be exploited, and remediating them autonomously with safeguards that let teams trust the results. The AI-ROC brings all of this together on one platform, with AI agents doing the work at machine speed and security teams in control of every decision that matters.

Every tool on the market can tell you how many exposures you have. The organizations that stay ahead in the frontier AI era will be the ones that can answer a harder question: how quickly can we turn exposure into verified risk reduction?

An AI-native Risk Operations Center. It detects exposures as soon as they are disclosed, proves which are exploitable, remediates with guardrails, and revalidates before closure. Security teams set policy and stay in control.

Can the Agents Patch Without Approval?

Only within the boundaries the team sets. Low-impact updates can be zero-touch. Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback is automatic if a service degrades. Nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

What Is Agentic ROC Studio?

A planned capability that will let teams build their own agents around existing runbooks, in plain language, with no scripting. Those agents will work alongside the Qualys agents and connect to third-party tools.

How Fast Does InstaScan Detect?

title: Reveal a key, not a payload: sending the ePBS payload before the reveal
description:
Author: @cskiraly
Thanks to @llewtae for the conversation that prompted this post. A narrower form of the idea is in my early draft Hiding the source of a segmented payload (October 2026): encrypted copies placed on a few nodes before the release, so that the source stays hidden. The form here, for the whole network and for time, first appeared as one line in my Devcon 8 talk, Big Blocks, Quick Slots, Fast Diffusion; this post explains it.
TL;DR
In Gloas (ePBS), the payload travels only once the builder reveals it. The builder has good reasons to wait after the beacon block, and every moment it waits comes out of the payload’s transfer time.
Pre-seeding removes that cost: once the block includes its bid, the builder sends the payload encrypted, and the reveal shrinks to a short message with a 32-byte key. The gain is the time from the block’s arrival to the reveal: up to about 3 s on 12 s slots with an early block, little with a late one.
The price: a builder that only has to send a key can decide later, so its free option to withhold grows. A builder with a private blob can already decide until the later blob deadline, by withholding the blob.
The budget
Gloas fixes the order, beacon block first and payload second, but not when the builder reveals. A payload revealed for a block that is then dropped shows its contents to whoever builds next, so the builder waits until attestations show the block will stay, and long enough to catch a proposer that equivocates; The Glamsterdam equation (2025) models the reveal the same way, as a builder delay after the attestation deadline. An honest builder may also withhold if the block arrived late and is not its head. A member of the payload timeliness committee (PTC) then votes the payload present only if it saw it before half the slot (PAYLOAD_DUE_BPS). Our earlier post assumed a reveal near 3 s, so a budget of about 3 s (Segment, code, push-pull, 2026). Attesters vote as soon as they receive the block, so an early block lets the builder be sure sooner, and a late one, as in timing games, leaves less time to gain.
A fast broadcast fits this budget with room: in simulation, SEACAST, a proposed broadcast protocol, gets 1 MiB, about five times today’s payload, to 99 % of an all-home network in about 0.6 s. The budget binds as payloads grow, slots shrink and uplinks thin: with 10 Mbps uplinks the same 1 MiB takes 1.8 s in that simulation, more than the 1.5 s the same slot fractions would leave on a 6 s slot. Meanwhile, the time between the block and the reveal carries nothing of the payload, which the bid’s block_hash has already fixed.
The idea
At bid time, the builder compresses the payload, encrypts it under a fresh key, and chunks and erasure-codes the ciphertext.
Once a valid block includes the bid, it pushes the ciphertext chunks, and nodes check and forward them.
At the reveal, it sends the key. Nodes check it and forward it at once; with enough chunks, they decrypt and check the envelope as Gloas specifies.
Why encrypt, when the block already commits? The commitment alone does not make plaintext safe: a block can still be dropped until it is attested. Encryption keeps waiting safe: if the block is dropped, the payload’s contents stay private, as an honest builder’s do in Gloas when it withholds. The same encryption keeps, and lengthens, the builder’s strategic option (below).
What changes in Gloas:
the bid commits to the ciphertext’s chunk root, as EIP-8411 at 41ba25cc does to a plaintext one, and to a hash of the key. With block_hash, this fixes what the key can open;
a topic for ciphertext chunks, checked against the root and forwarded only once a valid block includes the bid (EIP-8411 at 41ba25cc forwards chunks for any bid accepted on the bid topic), so no losing bid’s ciphertext travels;
a reveal message: the key and the builder’s signature over the key and the beacon block root, both checked before forwarding (the key against its hash); the envelope is encrypted without its beacon_block_root, as EIP-8411 chunks it;
a PTC member votes the payload present if the key and enough ciphertext reached it before the deadline and decrypt to an envelope that passes its checks; a wrong or missing key counts as a withheld payload;
after the reveal, a node that missed chunks can request the envelope by its beacon block root, as in Gloas.



Figure 1. The time the payload has to reach the nodes, in one 12 s slot. In Gloas as specified, it runs from the reveal to the payload deadline; pre-seeded, the encrypted payload has from the block to the deadline, and only the key waits for the reveal. The block is drawn at the slot’s start and the reveal at the attestation deadline, as assumed above: the largest gain. A later block, or an earlier reveal, leaves less.
The block-level access list. Gloas puts the BAL (EIP-7928) inside the payload; pre-seeded as above, it is encrypted with the rest. EIP-8146 at b6d3f2c6 would send it instead as a plaintext sidecar once the beacon block is published, arguing that state changes hold no signed transaction to unbundle; only the rest of the payload then needs encrypting. The two parts share the links from the block on, and one arriving early means the other arrives late (The payload and its BAL: how to split on the network?, 2026). Once published, a plaintext BAL exposes the block’s state accesses and post-transaction changes, even if the block is dropped. To hide it as well, a builder could pre-seed the BAL as it does the payload, under a key of its own; a PTC member would count it only if it had opened it and matched it to the bid’s BAL hash a second before the payload’s deadline, and nodes would gain time to prefetch state if it opens before the rest of the payload.
Why not something simpler
Pre-seed k−1 of the parity chunks and send the last one at the reveal. With Reed–Solomon over k data chunks, k−1 chunks cannot be decoded, but at every symbol offset they are k−1 equations in k unknowns: they give away all but one symbol in k, and one correct symbol from any other chunk decodes that offset. Some of what is left is public already, from the bid’s fields to transactions seen in the mempool. Mazorra, Öz, Schlegel and Wu (2025) describe the same move for blob columns, released “just below the threshold required for reconstruction”, as a way to lengthen the builder’s option. A one-time pad cannot help either: it hides perfectly only if it is as large as the payload (Shannon). A key is the computational route, and gives a short reveal.
What it costs
The builder’s option grows, on one route. Mazorra et al. find that the free option’s value, and how often it is used, grow with the window in which the builder can still decide; shortening the window helps, at a cost to scalability. Their window ends at the latest release of the blobs, whose deadline is later. A key’s time does not grow with the payload, so pre-seeding moves the latest payload reveal later by about the payload’s transfer time less a key’s. The blob route, to three quarters of the slot, is unchanged, and a withheld key keeps the payload hidden where withheld blobs leave it public. Moving the payload deadline earlier would offset the payload route only, and take back as much of the payload’s gain.
A withheld payload wastes its ciphertext’s bytes at every node, and stays hidden, though its length shows the compressed size; the builder pays its bid only if the block gathers enough attestations.
Early bytes share the links with the block and the attestations due at a quarter of the slot, so part of the head start can go to them.
Related work
Sending a block encrypted and revealing a short key later is not new: bloXroute (Klarman, Basu, Kuzmanovic and Sirer, 2018) reveals the key once its encrypted blocks have spread, its “minuscule size” letting it “quickly propagate”, to keep its network neutral. In Ethereum, encrypting the payload before its reveal has been proposed to take a choice away: from the MEV-Boost relay (Luhn, 2022; Noyes and Policharla, 2024, whose encrypted block is gossiped with the proposal and opened by the attestations), and from the ePBS builder (Shutter, 2025); Buterin (2022) placed encrypted coded chunks with a committee before the proposal. Per transaction, LUCID (2026) spreads sealed transactions ahead of a key revealed once the beacon block is trusted, and encrypted frame transactions (Thiery, 2026) check such a key against a commitment. Blob Streaming (2026) moves public blob data ahead of the critical path, and EIP-8146 (2026) the BAL. New here, as far as we found: the whole Gloas payload, under the builder’s own key, spread after the block so that its transfer runs ahead of the reveal, and what that does to the builder’s option.
Open questions
How much time is gained depends on when nodes hold the block, how long builders wait, and how fast a key spreads; it needs measuring.
Where the payload deadline should sit once the payload no longer waits for the reveal.
Blobs and self-builders. Encrypted blob columns would fail the KZG checks, which are against commitments to the plaintext, so blobs need their own answer; a self-builder may not need any of this.

title: NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public
description:
New Jersey law, like the law of most states, expressly permits the public to observe the closing of the polls and the counting of votes. But some New Jersey county election boards have policies which claim to prohibit the public from witnessing this process in both precinct polling places and vote centers, contrary to the […]
The post NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public appeared first on CITP Blog.
fullContent:
New Jersey law, like the law of most states, expressly permits the public to observe the closing of the polls and the counting of votes. But some New Jersey county election boards have policies which claim to prohibit the public from witnessing this process in both precinct polling places and vote centers, contrary to the law. I urge those county election boards to adjust their policies before the next election.

Voting machines (such as optical-scan tabulators) record votes internally as they are cast during the election, and at the end of election day the poll workers “close the polls.” That is, they instruct the voting machine to print the vote counts onto “poll tapes” and also write them into removable media (thumb drives). The poll tapes and thumb drives are transported to the county’s election office for uploading to an election management computer, but before they leave the polling place the poll tapes are signed (in pen) by election workers and they can be seen by witnesses. This is a useful protection against tampering in transit or in the election office.

Who is allowed to witness those poll tapes? In most states (the ones shown in green on this map), any member of the public can see them. But in a few states (the ones in red-brown on the map), you need to be a “credentialed pollwatcher” or “challenger”, that is, appointed by a political party or by a candidate to observe the polling place.

Credentialed pollwatchers (called challengers in some jurisdictions) sit at the voter check-in table all day, close enough to hear the voter’s name and address; they can see who votes, they can see that no one is stuffing unauthorized ballots into the voting machine, and generally observe that the election is conducted fairly. There are good reasons that arbitrary members of the public are not allowed to do that: it could intimidate voters or otherwise hinder the process of voting. So pollwatchers need credentials, formally requested from the Board of Elections by the political parties or candidates.

But after the polls close, it’s different. There are no more voters, and most states recognize that election transparency is well served by permitting the public to observe the vote count, as long as they don’t interfere.

When the Attorney General sent lawyers to watch me vote

Once upon a time, I was serving as an expert witness for some public-interest plaintiffs who were suing the State of New Jersey, in state court, over the use of paperless electronic voting machines. Back then, quite a few states used such machines, without any kind of paper trail, so if someone managed to install fraudulent software in the voting machine to report fake vote totals, there were no paper ballots that could be recounted. Now, only Louisiana uses those machines.

I wanted to observe the closing-of-the-polls procedure in my local polling place in the November 2008 general election. A few days before, I asked my county election officials about that, and was told that I couldn’t. Lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote to New Jersey’s Attorney General about this, and she wrote this brief letter:

Re: Observing the Announcement of Election Results

This is to confirm that under N.J.S.A. 19:16-2, the announcement of election results, at the close of the polls, shall be “open and public”, with the caveat that no one can interfere with the election officials.

Sincerely yours,

ANNE MILGRAM, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF NEW JERSEY

What happened next? On Tuesday morning, November 4th, 2008, I went to my usual polling place to vote, the elementary school gymnasium. As usual, there was the table where I signed the pollbook. As usual, sitting at that table were two poll workers (working for the county board of election) and poll watchers (representing the political parties). What was different this time was another table, off to the side, with two men in business suits, just watching.

That evening at 8pm, I went back to the polling place to observe. I brought a copy of my letter from the Attorney General, just in case. When I arrived, I told the poll worker that I’d like to observe. She told me that I wasn’t allowed. I was just about to pull out my hall pass letter from the A.G., when one of the men in suits came over and told the poll worker that I was allowed to watch.

Apparently, the A.G.’s office was so worried that I would cause some sort of trouble that they sent two staff attorneys to my polling place to sit there all day long. Well, they needn’t have bothered; I had no intention of causing trouble or interfering with election officials.

What the law says

The state law that Ms. Milgram referred to says,

19:16-2. Votes counted publicly without adjournment

The district board shall then proceed forthwith to count the votes for each candidate or proposition and shall complete such count without delay or adjournment. The counting shall be open and public, but not to the extent that the number present shall hinder, delay or inconvenience the election officers in counting the ballots and ascertaining the result.

This law comes from the days when there was a wooden ballot box, and the pollworkers in the precinct (the “district board”) would open the ballot box and count the votes. The official interpretation of this law in New Jersey, per the Attorney General’s letter in 2008, is that “counting shall be open and public” means that the procedures used in having the voting machines print out the poll tapes, and the viewing of those poll tapes, shall be open to the public.

In the present day

Before Election Day 2026, a New Jersey county election official told me that she believed the County Board of Election’s policy was to bar the public from the closing of the polls; only those with pollwatcher credentials would be admitted.

On election night, November 3rd at 8pm, members of the public were not permitted to observe polling places in Mercer County (Chestnut Street firehouse in Princeton) and in Somerset County (Finderne Rescue Squad building in Bridgewater). They were told they needed a pollwatcher credential.

So it appears that, in at least some parts of New Jersey, county Boards of Elections are unaware that NJSA 19:16-2 requires them to permit the public to observe the closing of the polls. This is not just a good idea: it’s the law. So I urge the county boards to adjust their rules, and inform pollworkers accordingly.

The post NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public appeared first on CITP Blog.

title: What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking!
description:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AI chatbots are an increasingly important source of political information, but audits of the information they provide typically don’t account for how the chatbot personalizes it based on a user’s previous interactions. For example, if you mentioned where you worked in a conversation, ChatGPT may remember that and factor it in when you […]
The post What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking! appeared first on CITP Blog.
fullContent:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AI chatbots are an increasingly important source of political information, but audits of the information they provide typically don’t account for how the chatbot personalizes it based on a user’s previous interactions. For example, if you mentioned where you worked in a conversation, ChatGPT may remember that and factor it in when you ask who to vote for. We ran a field audit with 160 US ChatGPT users in the final days before the 2026 midterms (October 31–November 3) in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, and Maine.

  • Each participant first told us about their politics (party, ideology, feelings toward each party, and Senate vote intention), their ChatGPT use, and their demographics. We never shared responses to these questions with ChatGPT, though it may have inferred some of this from their previous conversations.
  • Each participant asked the same election questions in their own ChatGPT account twice with memory on and twice with memory off. The questions covered Senate candidates’ positions, the current administration, voting advice, and local election news.
  • Answers were annotated for partisan slant by two AI judges from different companies (Anthropic and OpenAI). Each judge rated every answer from −3 (favors the Democratic side) to +3 (favors the Republican side) without knowing whether it was personalized.

We find that memory settings change the political information users receive when asking election-related questions:

  • Personalized responses contain more partisan slant. The average difference between personalized and non-personalized answers is 0.12 standard deviations (SD) higher than the difference between two non-personalized answers (p < 0.001). On the judges’ seven-point scale, that is roughly 0.1 points.
  • Personalized responses are slanted towards the user’s own party affiliation.When memory is turned on, answers move 0.10 standard deviations toward the participant’s side on average (p < 0.05), that is, toward the Democratic side for Democrats, and toward the Republican side for Republicans.
  • Personalized responses are slanted in subtle, not explicit ways. ChatGPT almost never tells people how to vote: the judges found an outright recommendation in 2 of 576 voting-advice answers. Instead, partisan slant differences seem to come from what answers emphasize, as we find no substantial differences in the sources or tone used.

This post presents preliminary analyses due to their timeliness. We are producing a more complete report with additional experiments and audits. The numbers here may change as we refine the methodology and data.

People Increasingly Ask AI About Politics, But Their Responses Have a Personalized Slant

AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have become an increasingly important source of political information. Depending on how you ask, between 8% (Pew Research) and 40% (NCoC / Carter Center) of US adults have used AI for election-related information. This may not count exposure to AI-generated summaries in search engines, which 65% of Americans report encountering at least sometimes.

Because of their rising importance to the democratic process, journalists and researchers have scrutinized the quality and impact of chatbot responses on politics, finding, for example, that interactions with chatbots may sway voter opinions (Potter et al. 2024, Lin et al. 2025), and that they may provide incorrect information, sometimes inventing electoral races or misidentifying candidates (Washington Post, 2026). However, existing audits of political content from these chatbots often lack external validity because they do not consider how people use AI chatbots (e.g., LLM Election Observatory).

Namely, these audits typically use API keys (simple ways to query ChatGPT in code) while ignoring that the actual commercial products users typically interact with, such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, are substantially different from models accessed through APIs (Kirgis et al. 2026, Wang et al., 2025). The chatbots, in fact, incorporate system-level instructions and have unique tools to let models access information. But most importantly, they have personalization mechanisms that adapt responses to individual users.

For example, ChatGPT’s memory system synthesizes previous conversations to tailor future responses, even when users did not explicitly ask it to remember specific pieces of information (OpenAI 2026). Even when memory is disabled, models can often see the user’s full name, aggregate location, and usage metadata. Recent studies found this personalization consequential to the chatbot’s responses, even when it does not directly reference it (Chang and Chen, 2026).

This raises an important question about the impact of LLMs on politics: to what extent does the information chatbots provide depend on who’s asking?

A Realistic Audit of ChatGPT Responses

To see what political information users got, we went to their accounts rather than to the API. Between October 31st and November 3rd, 2026, in the last days before the midterm elections, we recruited 160 US (self-reported) citizens living in five states with competitive Senate races (Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, and Maine; Princeton IRB 20343). We asked these participants to install a web extension that sent a battery of political questions through their own ChatGPT accounts and recorded the model’s replies. We summarize the experiment in the figure below.

We sent each question four times per user: twice with ChatGPT’s personalization on, so it could draw on the user’s memory, and twice with personalization off. Having two answers per memory setting also lets us compare variance between answers given with or without memory, since ChatGPT never gives exactly the same answer twice. Participants sent questions about candidates’ positions (“Where do the Senate candidates in Ohio stand on corporate corruption?”), the current administration (“How have the tariffs affected the country?”), voting advice (“I care most about my cost of living. Who should I vote for in the Senate race in Texas?”), and local election news (“What happened at Trump’s Port Huron rally?”). Expert political scientists working on our project curated the questions. Before sharing anything with us, participants read every answer and could hide any part of it, such as personal details. We also ran a scrubber to remove sensitive information.

To measure partisan slant, we had two LLMs from different companies, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) and GPT-6.1 (OpenAI), rate each answer from −3 (favors the Democratic side) to +3 (favors the Republican side). Each judge saw all four answers to a question together, in random order, without knowing which used memory. We also measured things that don’t require a judge, e.g., answer length, sources cited, which candidate is named first, and the tone used about each candidate. We use this data to measure the effect of personalization in answers, as we have, for each user, how ChatGPT would have answered the question with memory on and off.

Results: ChatGPT’s Answers Depend on Who’s Asking

We find that memory use shapes the political information users receive from ChatGPT. We present two key findings in this preliminary analysis, namely that 1) memory changes the slant of answers, most of all for news-related questions; and 2) that the change in answer slant leans toward the user’s own party.

Whether its memory was on or off, ChatGPT rarely gave direct advice on how people should vote: the judges found an outright endorsement of a candidate in only 2 of 576 voting-advice answers (both personalized!). Still, answers with memory differ significantly in structure; for example, they cited government websites slightly less often (−1.1 percentage points, p < 0.01) and were 3% shorter (7.5% for news-related questions). The sites ChatGPT cited lean no more to the left or right with memory on than off (classifying domains with the methodology from Robertson et al., 2018). Nor does its tone change: a sentiment model for political news (NewsMTSC) finds it describes each candidate just as positively or negatively either way.

Still, memory changes the political slant of what ChatGPT says. Answers with and without memory differ in slant by 0.12 SD more than two answers in the same setting (p < .001), a 20% increase over ChatGPT’s typical between-answer variation. The difference is largest for local election news, such as “What happened at Trump’s Port Huron rally?” or “What happened at Barack Obama’s Cleveland rally with Sherrod Brown?” (0.24 SD). For those questions, answers with and without memory differ by a point or more on our 7-point scale 38% of the time, compared with 24% for two answers asked the same way.

Finally, we find that, when memory is on, the slant of the answers moved 0.10 SD toward the participant’s own party (p < 0.05). On our 7-point scale, an answer with memory was at least a point closer to the user’s party than the answer without it 19% of the time, and at least a point further away 14% of the time. Democrats’ answers moved toward the Democratic side (−0.11 SD) and Republicans’ toward the Republican side (+0.08 SD), so answers with memory pulled the two parties 0.19 SD apart (p < .05). The effect is small, and the Republican shift alone is not statistically clear. But when we disaggregate by type of question, the two parties shift in different places: Democrats’ answers moved most in voting advice (−0.24 SD, p < 0.05), while Republicans’ moved most on local news (+0.31 SD, p < 0.05).

Some evidence of this shift appears even without the AI judges, based on which candidate an answer names first. For Democratic users, enabling memory reduced the share of answers listing the Republican candidate first from 56% to 48% (p < .01). For Republican users, the change was small and not statistically clear (59% to 56%).

So What? Auditing Chatbots as People Use Them

Chatbot audits have typically asked whether a model is “neutral,” whether, when asked a political question, it favors one side. Absolute neutrality is likely unattainable for normative political questions, such as whom to vote for or which policy is preferable, on which we lack consensus on evaluative criteria (Fisher et al., 2025). But our results suggest that ChatGPT does not attain a weaker standard: that the answer to a political question should not depend on who is asking it.

How chatbots should provide political information to those seeking it, and even whether they should at all, is a topic of ongoing debate. Still, we hope the results add nuance to this conversation by highlighting the limits of simple API-driven audits and the need to study chatbots as people actually use them.

The Algorithms+Elections Project at Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy studies how generative AI and social media platforms are reshaping the way voters find political information and form their views.

The post What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking! appeared first on CITP Blog.

title: XRP Ledger’s Big Bank Test Covered Only 2 of 10 Rules
description:
Summary CertiK checked two of ten GL1 principles. The public release discloses no findings. Issuers keep freeze and clawback powers. […]
The post XRP Ledger’s Big Bank Test Covered Only 2 of 10 Rules appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Summary

  • CertiK checked two of ten GL1 principles.
  • The public release discloses no findings.
  • Issuers keep freeze and clawback powers.
  • New amendments can outpace the attestation.

The XRP Ledger Foundation said on November 18 that XRPL is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have those two principles independently verified, citing a CertiK attestation report dated November 13.

Two principles verified, eight graded at home

The Foundation completed a self-attestation against all ten principles of GL1’s Market Infrastructure Toolkit. Its answers cover governance, legal basis, settlement finality, operational and cyber resilience, access and participation, and data and privacy. CertiK reviewed only the responses and evidence filed under Architecture and Resiliency. GL1’s toolkit website shows the same split.

What did CertiK find? The release doesn’t say. It publishes no findings, quotes no one from CertiK and leaves out the XRPL software version under review. Anyone who wants more than the headline has to ask for the report.

The harder part sits inside the framework. The toolkit builds on the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, the Digital Asset Securities Control Principles and the Global Blockchain Business Council’s risk mitigation framework, and many of its controls assume a single operator runs the network. XRPL has none. Where a control didn’t fit, the Foundation explained how protocol design, open-source governance, the amendment process and issuer compliance tools handle the same risk instead.

So a bank’s risk team isn’t reading a checklist. It’s reading a translation, and it has to judge whether each substitute does the work of the control it replaces.

XRPL also isn’t the only name on GL1’s list. Just one other entry carries a CertiK verification label, and it runs a permissioned network. That explains why the Foundation’s “first” claim leans so hard on the words “public, permissionless.”

Named on GL1’s toolkit page

Arc (Circle)
Base
Broadridge DLR
HSBC Orion
Kinexys by J.P. Morgan
Partior – CertiK-verified
Prividium (Matter Labs)
Solana
Tempo
T-REX Network
XRP Ledger – CertiK-verified

GL1 thanks these organisations for “self-attestations and/or feedback” and does not mark the status of the unlabelled entries.

Who backs GL1, and what they didn’t sign

The Monetary Authority of Singapore convened the original GL1 initiative with global banks and policymakers. On November 4, HSBC, Kinexys by J.P. Morgan, MUFG Bank, Societe Generale-FORGE and Standard Chartered turned it into an industry-led non-profit based in Singapore. The working group behind the toolkit includes the Bank of England, Banque de France and MAS.

Heavy names. None of them approved XRPL.

The Foundation’s release says so directly: the attestation isn’t certification, approval or endorsement by GL1, any central bank, regulator or participating institution, and it isn’t a finding that XRPL meets the standards the toolkit draws on. It tells institutions to run their own assessments.

Foundation Executive Director Brett Mollin pitched the exercise as an answer to fatigue. Institutions, he said, don’t need “another white paper” arguing that public ledgers can carry tokenized assets; they need evidence their compliance teams can map. Fair enough. But that map ends at the network. Follow one payment and you can see where the bank’s own work begins.

Who can move the bank’s token?

Picture a bank sending an issuer-backed dollar token to an approved counterparty. Before anything reaches the ledger, it needs answers. What does the token represent? What can the holder redeem? Who inside the bank may sign?

XRPL now gives it finer control over that last question. Permission Delegation went live on mainnet on October 8 through the PermissionDelegationV1_1 amendment, replacing an earlier version that never reached mainnet after a bug surfaced in testing. An account can hand a delegate up to ten specific permissions, so routine signing runs on limited keys while the master key stays offline. Delegates can’t change keys or grant themselves extra powers.

The protocol enforces each permission. The bank decides who holds them, how it guards the keys and what happens when an employee leaves. Coindoo’s look at XRPL’s new wallet controls walks through the setup.

In the ledger doesn’t mean paid

The bank submits. A success message comes back. Nothing has settled yet.

XRPL’s finality documentation separates that early response from the result recorded in a validated ledger, and validated ledgers hold failures too. Some failed transactions still pay a fee and land in the record. An operations system that spots the transaction in a ledger and stops checking could credit a customer for money that never moved.

So the bank’s software has to read the final result code and the balance changes the transaction actually made. Partial payments add a trap: the delivered amount can fall short of the amount field, and only the delivered figure counts.

Dropped connections cause the nastier problem, because the bank can’t tell whether the payment failed, succeeded or is still pending. XRPL’s submission guidance tells applications to give every transaction a last valid ledger, so a lost instruction expires at a known point, and to confirm the original’s fate before sending a replacement. Skip that check and the bank can pay twice.

READ MORE:

Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money

The issuer keeps a hand on the balance

The payment validates. Can the recipient move those tokens next week?

That depends on the issuer, not the network. Under XRPL’s freeze rules, an issuer can freeze a single holder’s trust line, which blocks that holder from sending the tokens anywhere except back to the issuer. A deep freeze also stops receiving and trading. A global freeze hits every holder of everything the issuer has issued. Issuers who want to give all of this up can set No Freeze, a permanent flag that only the master key can sign.

Clawback works on a stricter clock. An issuer has to switch it on before its account holds any trust lines, offers, escrows or similar objects, so it can’t bolt clawback onto a token already in circulation. Clawback and No Freeze can’t coexist, and neither tool touches XRP.

None of this rewrites history; a clawback is a fresh transaction. It does change what the bank’s customer actually holds. Those settings sit on the issuer’s account where anyone can query them, and they reveal more about one token’s risk than a network-wide attestation does.

Brazil shows the issuer side at work. In a September 29 announcement, Ripple and depository CSD BR said XRPL now mirrors records of BTG Pactual fund shares as Multi-Purpose Tokens. CSD BR’s systems remain the official record. The ledger lets authorized participants audit that the two match, and only Brazilian corporate and banking clients that clear KYC and anti-money-laundering checks can join.

CSD BR also keeps the power to freeze holdings or claw them back when a regulator or court orders it. Whatever the ledger shows, the depository’s register and Brazilian law decide ownership. Coindoo’s report on XRPL’s entry into Brazil’s fund system has the project background.

An attestation of a network that won’t sit still

XRPL changes through amendments. One takes effect after it holds support from more than 80% of trusted validators, meaning those on the default Unique Node List, for two straight weeks.

Those changes come often. Permission Delegation arrived on October 8. Within weeks, validators enabled fixCleanup3_4_0, which closed a gap that let a delegated burn permission create new tokens.

The Foundation says it intends to refresh its assessment as the toolkit evolves and new amendments activate. Today’s readers have a narrower problem. Because the release doesn’t name the software version CertiK reviewed, a risk team can’t tell which of this autumn’s changes the attestation covers. Ask for that first.

The post XRP Ledger’s Big Bank Test Covered Only 2 of 10 Rules appeared first on Coindoo.

title: Bullish Posts $576 Million Q3 Profit, but Adjusted Earnings Were Just $18.7 Million
description:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth. 
The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.
 Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026. 
Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline
Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA. 
Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results. 
The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.
Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results
Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA 
The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter. 
Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.
Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million. 
The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million. 
Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.
fullContent:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth.

The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.

Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline

Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA.

Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results.

The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.

Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results

Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA

The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter.

Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.

Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million.

The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million.

Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..

This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: WSDT introduces prop trading for crypto and tokenized US stocks
description: One-step challenges start at $19, with a free demo and weekly competitions available in the same trading terminal DUBAI, UAE, November 18, 2026 – WSDT is introducing its prop trading platform for cryptocurrency perpetual futures, gold and tokenized US stocks. Traders can access these markets through a single simulated account, with one-step evaluations starting at a one-time fee of $19 for a $1,500 account. The platform combines crypto perpetual futures, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, with xStocks instruments tracking companies such as Apple, NVIDIA and Tesla, alongside stock-index ETFs. Perpetual futures are contracts without an expiry date; xStocks track the prices of underlying shares or ETFs. On WSDT, these instruments are traded in a simulated environment, without ownership of the underlying shares or tokens. Positions across the markets share the same account balance and count toward the same evaluation. Traders can work across crypto and equity-linked instruments in one terminal while managing a single set of account limits. One evaluation, published trading rules A WSDT challenge tests trading performance against a 10% profit target, a 4% daily loss limit and a 6% maximum drawdown fixed against the starting account size. Traders must trade on at least four separate days, with no deadline to complete the evaluation. Account sizes range from $1,500 to $200,000, with fees varying by size. Traders who pass move to a funded-stage account, which is also simulated and retains the loss limits. They receive 80% of eligible profits under WSDT’s Provider Service Agreement. The evaluation fee pays for access to the challenge; it is not a trading deposit. Free ways to try the platform Registered users can open a free 14-day demo with a $100,000 simulated balance, without providing a payment card or making a deposit. The demo uses the same terminal as challenges, allowing traders to practice before entering an evaluation. Demo results do not qualify for payouts. WSDT also runs an ongoing weekly competition with free entry. Every participant starts with a $240,000 simulated balance, and the top three finishers receive challenge accounts. A new round opens each Monday at noon New York time. Winners must pass their awarded challenge before progressing to the funded stage. Registration, account options and full challenge rules are available on the WSDT website. About WSDT WSDT provides trader evaluation and educational services across crypto, gold and tokenized equity instruments. Built by TEFS, a prop trading firm established in 2017, it is operated by TEFS Marketing Management L.L.C. in Dubai, UAE. All WSDT trading accounts are simulated. Contact WSDT support@wsdt.com

title: Investment Scams Cost Americans $27,500,000 in Eight Months, Topping Online Purchase Fraud

fullContent:
Investment scams have cost Americans $27.5 million in reported losses over eight months, more than any other fraud type that commonly targets older adults.

Homewatch CareGivers says it analyzed Better Business Bureau Scam Tracker reports from January 1st to August 24th.

Online purchase fraud was the most reported scam, with 53,934 reports and $25 million in losses.

Phishing was second by volume, with 27,389 reports and $9 million in losses.

Investment scams ranked lower in volume, with 1,110 reports. Even so, their losses were the highest of any category in the study at $27.5 million.

“Although Online Purchase fraud and Phishing are the most commonly reported scams targeting seniors, Investment scams cost Americans more money. The Better Business Bureau tracked 1,110 Investment scams in our data period, and there were 15 types of scams that were more prevalent than this. But because of the high figures involved in investment scams, the total reported loss equals $27.5 million — three times the cost of Phishing to scam victims and dozens of times the cost of most other fraud types.”

Las Vegas had the highest rate of scams that commonly target seniors among 25 major cities, at 97 per 100,000 residents over an eight-month period.

Victims in Houston lost $1,009,000 to investment fraud, representing 9% of the total losses in the fraud category in Texas.

New Hampshire had the highest rate among states, with 816 reports, or 58 per 100,000 residents.

The figures include reports from victims of all ages, not just seniors.

The post Arthur Hayes Says Anthropic IPO Could Trigger Bitcoin Rally: Do the Numbers Agree? appeared first on 99Bitcoins.
fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC USD) trades near $64,000 on Wednesday, November 18, the day before Anthropic’s shares start trading on Nasdaq, and BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes says the listing will set Bitcoin’s direction. If the Anthropic IPO pops, Hayes told the New Era Finance Podcast, “it’s game back on. It’s long everything. Risk on.” He added: “Bitcoin’s going to go up too.”

It’s a clean, testable call. So we tested it against the last 12 big IPOs. When a listing jumped 20% or more on its first day, BTC USD was up a median 2% a month later. When it didn’t, Bitcoin was up a median 12%.

Bitcoin needs a lift. It is down 13% in a week, and the Fear & Greed Index, a daily sentiment gauge from 0 to 100, sits at 11, deep in “extreme fear.”

So does an Anthropic pop really mean a Bitcoin rally?

BTC USD After 12 Big IPOs: The Pops Didn’t Pay

We took 12 large listings since 2019, from Uber to SpaceX. For each one, we compared the stock’s first-day close with its IPO price, then measured Bitcoin from the listing day to 7 and 30 days later, using Binance’s daily closes.

  • Big pops: six IPOs jumped 20% or more on day one: Figma, Circle, Airbnb, Snowflake, Rivian and Arm. A week later, Bitcoin was up after four of them, but only by a median 0.9%. A month later, the median was 2%.
  • Small or no pops: after the other six, Bitcoin was up 30 days later five times, with a median gain of 12%. Uber fell 8% on its first day in 2019, and Bitcoin rose 20% over the next month.
  • The closest case: SpaceX gained 19% on its first day in June. BTC USD was flat a week later and flat a month later.

Twelve listings is a small sample, and the market around each one mattered more than the stock. Airbnb’s +120% month came in the December 2020 bull run, and Rivian’s −27% month came at the November 2021 top. What the numbers don’t show is a link between a hot debut and a Bitcoin rally.

DISCOVER: Bitcoin Below Its 200-Week Average for the First Time Since 2022: Is a Drop to $50K Coming or a Historic Buying Opportunity?

Hayes Sees Anthropic as a Test of Risk Appetite

Hayes’s point is less about Anthropic than about mood. A strong debut for the largest AI listing would show that investors are willing to buy risk again, and Bitcoin usually trades as a risk asset. On November 11, he wrote on X that he was adding crypto exposure ahead of the listing, while keeping his positions small enough to exit quickly.

Demand for the shares looks strong. Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share in its roadshow announcement. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that demand could push the price above $80. On Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange, a pre-IPO contract on the shares trades about 24% above that.

The other side is money. At the top of the range, the listing raises about $64 billion. Some of that cash comes from investors selling other assets, and Bitcoin slid about 20% in the weeks before SpaceX’s record listing in June.

DISCOVER: Top 20 Crypto to Buy in 2026

BTC USD Price Analysis: $65,500 Is the First Test

On the daily chart, BTC USD trades at $64,069. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,755, and its 200-day EMA at $75,753.

  • Resistance: $65,500, a level Bitcoin bounced from in February, March and April and was turned back from in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300, which capped prices in March and held as a floor in April, May and September.
  • Support: $62,300, Sunday’s low. Bitcoin bounced near it in February, June, July and August. Below it, $57,800, the July low and the bottom of the past year.
Path What has to happen Next stop
Bullish A strong Anthropic debut and a daily close above $65,500 $74,300, the March-September level
Sideways A modest debut, price between $62,300 and $65,500 A range near current levels
Bearish A weak debut or a daily close below $62,300 $57,800, the July low

Hayes may still be right about the mood. But if history is a guide, a big Anthropic pop is not enough on its own. BTC USD needs buyers to come back to crypto, not just to AI stocks.
